editorials.title: An Indian writer
editorials.passage:
The beginning of the birth-centenary celebrations of Rahi Masoom Raza lets us return to a writer whose literary stature has, paradoxically, been obscured by his enormous success outside literature. For the Indian public, Raza remains the man who wrote the memorable dialogues of B. R. Chopra’s Mahabharat. Others remember his long and successful association with Hindi cinema. Both are important parts of his achievement. But before everything else, Rahi Masoom Raza was a major writer. Aadha Gaon, Topi Shukla, Os Ki Boond and Katra Bi Arzoo place him securely among the significant Indian novelists of the second half of the twentieth century. 

The centenary is therefore an opportunity not simply to commemorate a celebrated cultural personality but to read Raza seriously again. Among these works, Aadha Gaon alone would have been sufficient to establish his literary reputation. It belongs to that relatively small group of Indian novels in which a particular locality becomes a means of understanding an entire historical transformation. Premchand had accomplished something comparable through the villages and small towns of North India; Phanishwar Nath Renu would make the apparently peripheral world of north Bihar central to modern Hindi fiction. Raza’s Gangauli, rooted in the Ghazipur region of eastern Uttar Pradesh, similarly becomes much more than the setting of a story. 

Through it he examines community, caste, family, language, memory, nationalism and Partition. To call Aadha Gaon simply a Partition novel is to diminish it. Partition provides the great historical rupture around which the novel moves, but Raza’s deeper subject is the transformation of a social world. Gangauli is neither an idyllic advertisement for what is now conveniently called composite culture nor a society permanently divided into antagonistic religious communities. It contains caste, hierarchy, patriarchy, prejudice and conflict. Yet people also inhabit overlapping worlds of neighbourhood, kinship, locality, language and memory. They possess several identities simultaneously. Raza’s extraordinary achievement is to show how modern politics begins to reorganise these relationships. 

Large political arguments gradually enter the village. Categories produced elsewhere acquire local force. People who had known one another through a dense network of everyday relations encounter each other through the abstraction of communal identity. Partition in Aadha Gaon is therefore not merely the division of territory. It is also a transformation of consciousness. That insight explains why the novel has lost none of its relevance. Raza understood something fundamental about identity politics: human societies are usually more complicated than the political categories through which they are mobilised. When one identity begins to demand exclusive loyalty, older and more intricate forms of belonging can rapidly become fragile. 

This concern extends beyond Aadha Gaon. Topi Shukla examines friendship, prejudice and the uneasy position of individuals who refuse to fit comfortably within communal expectations. Os Ki Boond returns to the anxieties produced by Partition and belonging. Katra Bi Arzoo moves into another social landscape, but its concern with ordinary lives caught within larger political processes remains recognisably Raza’s. Even when his settings changed, his deepest literary question remained remarkably consistent: what happens to human relationships when ideology, power and history begin imposing simplified identities upon complicated lives? There was another reason why Raza could portray this world with such intimacy: language. 

Much recent discussion of him has concentrated on whether particular works were originally written in the Urdu script or Nagari. The recovery of original manuscripts in the Perso-Arabic script is unquestionably important. Such material can clarify the textual history of his novels and should lead to reliable critical editions. But the centenary would become unnecessarily narrow if this discovery were allowed to define Raza’s literary identity. The language of Aadha Gaon itself warns us against such simplification. Its characters do not speak according to the classifications of literary institutions. 

Their speech carries Bhojpuri rhythms, Hindustani usage, Persian-Arabic vocabulary, local idiom, affection, abuse and the distinctive cadence of eastern Uttar Pradesh. Raza’s literary language arose from a living multilingual society before it entered the categories called Hindi and Urdu. Bhojpuri is particularly important here. Discussions about Raza frequently move between Hindi and Urdu as though these were his only two linguistic worlds. They were not. Ghazipur and the wider Bhojpuri-speaking region supplied the soil of his imagination. Once this is recognised, many apparent linguistic contradictions disappear. Raza could remain deeply attached to Urdu and its literary culture while writing works that entered the Hindi literary canon because he did not imagine languages as sealed cultural territories. His own reflections on language were remarkably clear. 

He regarded Hindavi, Hindi, Urdu-e-Mu’alla and Urdu as names emerging at different moments within a long and intertwined linguistic history. He liked to remind readers that Jayasi could write Awadhi in the Persian script while Tulsidas wrote Awadhi in Nagari. Script, in other words, did not determine the identity of a language. Raza was not demanding the abandonment of the Perso-Arabic script. His argument was more interesting: no script should become the exclusive gateway through which a language must be approached. The discovery of his Urdu-script manuscripts therefore enriches textual scholarship without overturning our understanding of Raza. 

Manuscripts tell us how texts travelled from composition to publication. Literary history must ask a larger question: what kind of imagination produced those texts? For Raza, that imagination was inseparable from the historical experience of the Gangetic plains. The memory of 1857 remained part of the region’s cultural landscape. It survived through histories, local traditions, family memories and later nationalist interpretations. One need not romanticise 1857 as an uncomplicated moment of Hindu-Muslim unity to recognise its importance in the making of a shared historical consciousness. Raza inherited a region in which religion, language, caste and locality had interacted for centuries, sometimes violently and often creatively. His fiction emerged from an awareness of this accumulated history. 

This helps explain his transition from literature to Bombay cinema. It is tempting to divide Raza’s career into two lives ~ the serious novelist and the professional film writer. The division is misleading. Bombay enlarged his audience, but it did not fundamentally alter the questions that interested him. Popular culture could also become a medium through which India talked to itself. The image of the road in Naya Daur provides a useful metaphor for the cultural world Raza inhabited. The film is usually remembered for its conflict between machines and labour, but its road can be built only through cooperation and the resolution of local antagonisms. Progress is not simply technological; people must discover ways of working with their neighbours. 

Much of Raza’s writing performed an analogous task. It built roads between cultural worlds that modern politics increasingly wished to separate. He carried an unusual independence into Bombay as well. Amit Khanna has recalled an episode involving Dilip Kumar and Sagina: when changes were sought, Raza was unwilling to accommodate the wishes of a major star, and Khanna respected his position rather than agreeing to replace him. Whatever the everyday compromises required by the film industry, Raza did not easily surrender the independence of a writer. And then came Mahabharat. The extraordinary popularity of B. R. Chopra’s television serial transformed Raza into a household name. Yet the question that followed him ~ how could a Muslim write the dialogues of the Mahabharata? ~ reveals more about modern India’s anxieties than about Raza. 

He famously regarded himself as a Gangaputra. The epic did not represent for him an alien religious territory into which a Muslim writer required special permission to enter. It belonged to the civilisational world in which he had grown up. History supports that instinct. The Mahabharata had travelled through Persian and Urdu intellectual traditions long before television arrived. Indian civilisation had never organised its texts according to the rigid cultural ownership that later politics sometimes imposed upon them. Raza’s participation in Mahabharat was therefore less anomalous than the surprise surrounding it suggests. Nor should the serial itself be turned into the achievement of a solitary writer. 

B. R. Chopra’s vision, Pandit Narendra Sharma’s conceptual contribution, researchers, scenario writers and other collaborators were important; the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute’s Critical Edition was among the significant textual resources used by the production. The making of the serial deserves serious scholarly reconstruction. Raza’s achievement lay elsewhere. He found a language through which an ancient epic could speak to a late-twentieth-century mass audience without becoming merely archaic or merely colloquial. The great moral problems remained intact ~ power and legitimacy, justice and humiliation, loyalty and conscience, duty and political ambition. 

In that respect, Mahabharat was not as far removed from Aadha Gaon as it initially appears. Both deal with societies under enormous strain; both ask what happens when inherited relationships confront political conflict; both resist simple moral categories. This is the Rahi Masoom Raza whom the centenary should restore. His journey from Ghazipur to Aligarh and eventually Bombay belongs to the history of modern Indian intellectual life. His elder brother Moonis Raza’s distinguished academic career forms another part of the same remarkable family history. Rahi’s own encounters and disagreements within literary and institutional worlds also deserve careful archival reconstruction. 

Rather than allowing either Hindi or Urdu establishments to claim or reject him retrospectively, scholars should examine how he actually negotiated these worlds. There is consequently much useful work that the centenary celebrations can initiate. Raza’s manuscripts should be preserved and critically edited. His correspondence and private papers should be made accessible. His relationship with Aligarh deserves fuller study. His enormous body of film writing requires documentation. The production history and textual foundations of Mahabharat invite serious research. Above all, his novels should return to the centre of discussion. That last task matters most. A centenary can easily become a sequence of ceremonial events in which a familiar name is repeatedly invoked while the books themselves remain unread. Raza deserves something better. 

He needs to be restored to the company of the major writers through whom twentieth-century India understood itself. It would therefore be unfortunate if the centenary became primarily an argument over whether Rahi Masoom Raza belonged to Hindi or Urdu. He belonged profoundly to both, but his imagination exceeded both literary establishments. Bhojpuri Ghazipur, Urdu poetry, Hindi fiction, Aligarh, Bombay cinema, the memories of Partition and the world of the Mahabharata could coexist within him because he did not understand Indian identity as a choice between mutually exclusive inheritances. 

The most valuable achievement of the centenary would thus be not merely the recovery of Raza’s manuscripts but the recovery of Raza himself: a great novelist, an independent intellectual and a writer whose Indian identity required neither apology nor explanation. At a time when languages, histories and cultural traditions are once again being assigned exclusive owners, reading Rahi Masoom Raza may remind us that some of India’s finest literature was created precisely by refusing those boundaries. 

(The writer is Professor of History, Rabindra Bharati University)

editorials.title: What gives us the right to judge?
editorials.passage:
We are all judges. We judge people by what they wear, how they speak, what they eat, where they live, how they spend their money and whom they choose to spend their time with. We judge decisions, relationships, governments, institutions, countries and events unfolding thousands of kilometres away. We judge books by their covers, people by their photographs and increasingly, entire lives by a few seconds of video. Judgement is perhaps one of the most effortless things human beings do. 

But there is a rather important distinction we rarely stop to make: having an opinion is not the same as having the capacity to judge well. A judge, after all, is not simply someone who knows the law. Society does not hand someone a judicial position merely because that person has read enough legal books. There are qualifications, training, procedures, standards of evidence, principles of impartiality and mechanisms of review. A judge is expected to listen, examine, distinguish fact from assertion, consider competing arguments and importantly, give reasons for a decision. In other words, the system recognises something rather fundamental: judgement is a responsibility. 

And yet, outside a courtroom, we appoint ourselves judges with remarkable enthusiasm. No qualifications required. No evidence required. No hearing of the other side required. Sometimes not even the complete sentence is required. We hear half a conversation and reach a conclusion. We see an action and decide what kind of person must have performed it. We encounter a decision whose circumstances we know nothing about and immediately pronounce it sensible or foolish, selfish or generous, intelligent or absurd. Perhaps this is where we need to pause. Because we very often do not know where the individual is coming from. 

We do not know what happened before the conversation began. We do not know what preceded the sentence we heard. We do not know what the person has been carrying silently. We do not know the circumstances behind the decision that appears irrational to us. We often judge a sentence without having heard the conversation that produced it, an action without knowing the circumstances that preceded it, and a person without knowing the life that shaped them. Yet we dive in. 

Perhaps human beings are uncomfortable with uncertainty. We like explanations. We like neat boxes labelled right and wrong, sensible and foolish, good and bad. Context complicates those boxes. Understanding takes time. Judgement takes seconds. There is also something strangely satisfying about reaching a conclusion. It gives us the feeling that we understand. But certainty and understanding are not necessarily the same thing. Consider how often we judge someone’s behaviour without knowing their circumstances. A person who seems rude may be exhausted. 

Someone who appears withdrawn may be struggling with something we cannot see. Someone who makes a decision we consider irresponsible may be dealing with choices we have never had to make. Someone who reacts strongly to a seemingly ordinary comment may be responding not merely to those words, but to a history attached to them. We do not need to excuse every behaviour. Nor should empathy mean abandoning accountability. There are actions that deserve criticism and decisions that must be challenged. But fair criticism requires knowledge. And that is the distinction worth making. 

Judgement should not be confused with condemnation. A considered judgement asks questions before reaching a conclusion. What are the facts? What is the context? What might I be missing? Have I heard the other side? Am I relying on evidence, or merely on an assumption that happens to fit my existing beliefs? Perhaps most importantly: what do I not know? That last question may be one of the most powerful forms of intellectual humility. We live in an age in which everyone has access to more information than any generation before us - and yet access to information can create the illusion of understanding. 

A headline becomes knowledge. A short video becomes evidence. A social media post becomes a complete account of an event. We consume fragments and manufacture wholes. The same applies to public life. Citizens have every right to question governments, institutions and public decisions. Indeed, a healthy democracy depends upon it. But there is a difference between scrutiny and instant verdict. To question is to seek understanding. To judge without sufficient knowledge is simply to declare a conclusion. Perhaps we should apply to our everyday lives some of the discipline we expect from a courtroom. Not literally, of course. We cannot conduct a trial before deciding whether someone’s new shirt is questionable. 

But we could introduce a little more restraint. We could listen a little longer. We could ask one more question. We could resist the temptation to fill gaps in knowledge with assumptions and perhaps we could occasionally say those three wonderfully liberating words: “I don’t know.” There is no weakness in that sentence. In fact, there may be considerable wisdom in it. The truly thoughtful person is not the one who has an opinion about everything. It is the one who knows when an opinion is informed, when it is instinctive, and when it is simply premature. Good judgement, therefore, may have less to do with knowing all the answers and much more to do with knowing the limits of what we know. 

It requires knowledge, certainly. But it also requires perspective, patience, experience, empathy and the willingness to reconsider our conclusions when new information arrives. And perhaps the rarest quality of all: the ability to change one’s mind without feeling that one’s dignity has been diminished. After all, changing one’s mind because one has learnt something new is not inconsistency. It is growth. Maybe this is why the formal world of judging surrounds judgement with so many safeguards. The system knows that human beings have biases, preferences, emotions and blind spots. Rules exist not because judges are incapable of judgement, but because even capable people need protection from the limitations of being human. 

Perhaps the rest of us could use a few such safeguards too. Before judging someone’s clothes, perhaps we could remember that we do not know their circumstances. Before judging someone’s life, perhaps we could remember that we have not lived it. Before judging someone’s words, perhaps we could listen to the conversation that came before them. Before judging a public event, perhaps we could find out what we actually know and what we merely believe we know. And before judging another human being, perhaps we could ask one deceptively simple question: Do I know enough to judge? The answer may sometimes be yes. But I suspect that, surprisingly often, it will be no and perhaps that is not a failure of judgement at all. Perhaps knowing when not to judge is the beginning of wisdom. 

(The writer is a certified yoga teacher, and heads marketing in a multinational company)

editorials.title: Protect our kids too
editorials.passage:
Twenty-nine U.S. states took on social media giants, accusing them of deliberately designing their platforms to be addictive and harmful to children. On August 26, Meta agreed to introduce stronger safeguards for teenagers on Facebook and Instagram, including a two-hour daily usage limit. Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube are expected to follow suit. In all, 47 American states agreed to the primary multi-state settlement, under which Meta will pay up to $16.7 billion and introduce new safeguards for users under 18. 

The most prominent change is a two-hour daily usage limit for minors on Facebook and Instagram (excluding direct messaging), which can only be modified by parents. Meta will also implement automatic overnight lockouts, offer teenagers a non-personalized chronological feed instead of algorithmic recommendations, and strengthen its age-verification systems under the oversight of an independent court-appointed auditor. “Protect our kids too.” Within 24 hours, the European Union (EU) had new “exchanges” with Meta, demanding similar safeguards. European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier said, “Now it is for the company to offer these commitments in the European Union to protect our kids here too.” 

The EU had already, in April, found Meta in preliminary breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for failing to prevent children under 13 from accessing Instagram and Facebook. So where is India in this global reckoning? India is home to over 47 crore children aged 0-18 years. One in five children on the planet lives here. They are just as susceptible, if not more so, given weaker institutional safeguards, to the same algorithmic harms. The dangers are not abstract; smartphones are increasingly becoming a serious threat to children's psychological and social development. Over the past two years, society has been shaken by horrific incidents: the killing of a 10-year-old girl by a 14-year-old boy in Hyderabad; the alleged sexual assault of a nine-year-old girl in Telangana by 12-year-old boys; and the rape and murder of an eight-year-old girl in Andhra Pradesh by three 14-year-old boys. 

These are just examples from two states. News reports indicate these kids were heavily exposed to pornography and violent content through smartphones. A LocalCircles survey found that one in two Indian parents had seen their children exposed to inappropriate content online. Constant exposure to violent and sexually explicit content normalises cruelty and gradually erodes children’s natural empathy. Australia banned social media for kids under 16, and Indonesia, Brazil, and Turkey have set strict age limits. The UK, Canada, and the EU are also forcing tech companies to verify users' ages. India has so far remained passive on implementing similar social media restrictions. 

In addition, India’s proposed framework must also confront four more major threats: adult pornography, graphic violent content, short-video traps, and gaming-betting hybrids. Adult Pornography: The U.S. Supreme Court settled the adult-privacy-versus-child-safety debate in Free Speech Coalition, Inc. v. Paxton (2025), upholding age verification. India must mandate effective age-assurance checks (such as biometric estimation or ID verification) as seen in the UK and France - abandoning the current ‘click-away’ self-attestation with penalties for platforms serving minors. Graphic violent content: Australia's Online Safety Codes require proactive detection before content reaches a child. 

India's current framework requires platforms to act only after actual knowledge, failing to prevent initial harm. A ‘Good Samaritan’ clause, similar to Article 7 of the EU’s DSA, would protect platforms that voluntarily remove harmful content, removing any disincentive against proactive moderation. Short-video traps: In K.G.M. v. Meta and Google, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable for negligence over their addictive features like infinite scroll and autoplay, awarding $6 million to a young woman. The current Meta settlement is directly connected to this case, holding platforms accountable for product design rather than just user-generated content. 

Indian children deserve similar accountability. Gaming-betting hybrids: India's Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 is silent on child-protection provisions. Mandatory cooling-off periods and spending caps must apply to online and offline games alike. Loot boxes and predatory monetization are classified as gambling and restricted or banned under consumer protection laws in Belgium, the Netherlands, South Korea and China. The EU’s DSA targets a broader category called ‘social media plus,' which includes video games, chat apps, and AI companions that act like friends. 

The UK’s Online Safety Act, paired with the Children’s Code, reduced traffic to major pornography sites by 77 per cent. China has implemented a ‘Minor Mode’ built into phone hardware that blocks internet access between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. At least 79 countries restrict smartphones in schools. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 imposes a ‘parental consent’ model, but parents under social or peer pressure may simply consent their children onto any platform. The Economic Survey 2025-26 even suggested that schools should consider allowing only basic phones. 

This issue should be treated as a serious public-health and social crisis, much like Covid-19, and discussed urgently by legislatures. The Meta settlement is a turning point: children's well-being is worth more than platform profits, and no corporation is too large to be held accountable. In addition, India needs transformative laws that regulate not just social media but the entire ecosystem of platforms that profit from our children's attention. The EU did not wait. It demanded that its children receive the same protections. India must now make the same demand: “Protect our kids too.” 

(The writer is co-founder of the 51ABI Foundation and can be reached at srinivasmadhav.india@gmail.com)

editorials.title: Death Beyond Music
editorials.passage:
The killing of Manipuri guitarist Chongtham Vikram Singh in Delhi should not be allowed to become another crime story that briefly captures public attention before disappearing into the news cycle. It raises a more uncomfortable question: who is entitled to feel completely at home in India’s capital? Singh was 54, a musician and teacher who had spent decades building a life through music. His journey from Manipur’s emerging rock culture to Kolkata and eventually Delhi was, in its own quiet way, a story of India becoming more connected. His death exposes how fragile those connections can remain. 

According to police and his family, Singh objected to men allegedly making noise and drinking outside his apartment. What followed was an assault that ended with his death in hospital. Seven men and a juvenile have been arrested. The investigation will have to establish exactly what happened and why. That last question matters enormously. There is, so far, no evidence cited by police establishing a racial motive. That must be respected. It would be irresponsible to convert suspicion into fact. Yet it would be equally irresponsible to ignore why Singh’s killing has resonated so strongly across the North-east. For years, people from the region living in Indian metropolitan cities, especially Delhi, have complained of racial slurs, stereotyping, harassment and violence. 

The significance of this case therefore lies partly in the gap between the immediate criminal facts and the social environment in which such incidents occur. Delhi is populated by people from every part of India. But geographical integration has not always produced social integration. Someone from Manipur can live in Delhi for decades, work, raise a family and contribute to its cultural life, yet still be made to feel foreign because of appearance, accent or ethnicity. The answer cannot be to presume that every crime involving a Northeastern Indian is racially motivated. Nor can it be to dismiss concerns about racial discrimination whenever motive is difficult to prove. 

Police investigations must establish facts, while governments and institutions must address the broader pattern independently of individual criminal cases. This means better recording and investigation of suspected racial abuse, greater sensitivity within policing, and sustained efforts to confront the stereotypes that make Indians from the North-east targets of casual discrimination. Educational institutions, workplaces, landlords and political leaders also have a role. Singh’s widow has made the most important distinction: the family wants justice, not revenge. 

Justice requires the attackers to be held accountable if the evidence establishes their guilt. But justice for Singh should also mean refusing to treat the anxieties exposed by his death as somebody else’s problem. A guitarist who spent his life getting different sounds to work together became, in death, a reminder of how divided Indian society can still be. The question Singh’s killing leaves behind is therefore larger than who committed one brutal assault. It is whether India’s promise of belonging extends equally to every Indian ~ especially when they look different from those around them.

editorials.title: Oily bargain
editorials.passage:
Venezuela’s oil industry needs foreign capital, technology and competent management. Few would dispute that. After years of mismanagement, corruption, sanctions and economic collapse, restoring production could generate jobs, government revenue and the resources needed to rebuild a devastated country. The difficulty is not the investment. It is the political bargain accompanying it. The United States has secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven reserves through an arrangement centred on North American Blue Energy Partners, which has received concessions covering 17 oilfields. The proposed investment could approach $100 billion. 

Washington says the arrangement is part of a broader plan of stabilisation, reconstruction and eventual democratic transition. On paper, this could be transformative. Venezuela currently produces only a fraction of the oil it once did. If American capital and expertise can restore output, the country could finally convert its extraordinary natural wealth into productive investment rather than political patronage. But Venezuela’s people did not elect the government negotiating this arrangement. Nicolás Maduro was removed by the United States in January. His former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, now heads the interim government, but no date has been fixed for elections. 

Donald Trump has said Venezuela is not yet ready for them. Rodríguez has promised that elections will eventually occur, without specifying when. That creates a dangerous incentive. The more valuable the new oil arrangement becomes, the greater Washington’s interest in political stability around it. And the more revenue and power the interim authorities acquire from revived oil production, the less obvious their incentive to hurry towards an election that could remove them. This does not mean Washington has deliberately abandoned Venezuelan democracy. Nor does it mean the oil deal cannot benefit ordinary Venezuelans. But foreign investment on this scale requires legal certainty, political legitimacy and public confidence. 

María Corina Machado has argued that only a democratic government can provide the stability required for sustained investment. There is also an unresolved legal question. Critics say the agreement may conflict with Venezuelan constitutional and legal requirements, including questions over the absence of a public tender and the length of the proposed concessions. Rodríguez has disputed the White House’s description of a 100-year concession, saying licences would be limited to 25 years. That matters because oil contracts can outlive governments. A concession lasting decades is not an ordinary commercial transaction. It can shape a country's economic and political choices for generations. America therefore faces a test of its own making. 

If it genuinely wants Venezuela to become democratic, prosperous and sovereign, it should welcome scrutiny of the deal rather than fear it. The ultimate legitimacy of the oil industry must come from Venezuelans themselves. Otherwise, Washington risks creating a paradox: using Venezuela’s oil to rebuild the country while creating reasons to postpone giving Venezuelans control over their own political future. For a nation emerging from authoritarian rule, that would be an extraordinary way to begin its democratic transition.

editorials.title: Ark of Atrocity
editorials.passage:
We had returned, content, from a screening of Dil Chahta Hai and parked in the driveway when I heard CNN playing on the small television in my mother’s room which was unusual because it was the time that she usually watched her serials. I peeped in through the bedroom window that overlooked the driveway and saw the second plane fly into the South Tower. I spent the rest of the evening trying to call New York to discover the whereabouts of my nephew who worked in one of the smaller buildings of the World Trade Center and learnt afterwards that he had been late to work and was en route in the subway when the planes struck.

The next August, we moved to New York for a couple of years and the first week we were there, we visited Ground Zero. I don’t remember much, if anything, of the scene there, just lots of black net and sheeting that obscured pretty much everything. PS 321, the public school my children attended in Brooklyn, still had a banner draped from its roof with “ una familia ” or “a family” emblazoned on it in several languages, including Arabic.

In most ways, at least to the outsider, the city seemed normal given what had happened a year ago. Some parents at the school spoke of leaving New York to leave the trauma of 9/11 behind but for the most part, the tenor of our life there was set by play dates, PTA meetings and the ordinary business of raising children. The people we met in the neighbourhood were uniformly kind and welcoming and apart from the century-old plumbing in our shared brownstone, we had no complaints.

The one fly in our ointment was the journalism that America produced. This was ironical because when I heard that my wife was about to be temporarily posted to New York, my first thought was that I’d finally get to read first-rate newspapers and magazines routinely. The New York Times and The New Yorker would become synchronised with my life, not back issues I caught up with in libraries. I hadn’t bargained on 9/11 making them unreadable.

I had a preview of the sheep-like stupidification of journalism in Narendra Modi’s India a dozen years before it happened here in, of all places, New York. This was that patriotic time when ornaments of the liberal press like Judith Miller in The New York Times and David Remnick in The New Yorker were making the case for invading Iraq. Miller wrote detailed scoops about how Saddam Hussein was buying aluminium tubes for nuclear weapons. Colin Powell stood up in the UN Security Council and solemnly told the world that Saddam had quantities of powdered anthrax that could sow death and terror across the world. He held up an empty glass vial to illustrate how much destruction the dictator could wreak with a little ampoule.

Every desi who watched Powell’s telecast performance knew he was lying. We didn’t have any special insight into intelligence about weapons of mass destruction, WMDs in the shorthand of the time, but we knew that netas used silly props like that vial to make their lies sound plausible. Americans were clearly less cynical about their leaders because the next day’s newspapers were full of ‘if Powell says there’s evidence, then Saddam must have WMDs’. In fact, there was no evidence at all, except for that vial prop and a sketchy schematic of a long, truck-like vehicle that was meant to be a mobile laboratory capable of brewing quantities of anthrax and other toxins.

Powell would later call his presentation a blot on his career and a major intelligence failure. This was shameless buck-passing. The failure was his; his political masters — George W. Bush, Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney — wanted to go to war so Powell found them a ‘smoking gun’ by choosing to believe the lies that Ahmed Chalabi and other Iraqi expatriates were peddling. Miller’s defence of her credulous reporting was a damning but representative sample of American journalism at the time. She said, years later, that she “was accurately conveying wrong information”. Miller argued that her job was to report the consensus of the intelligence community, not to second-guess it. She also knew it in her gut: “I knew Saddam Hussein, he’d thrown me in jail (years earlier). I knew how horrible he was... I made the same intellectual leap that the analysts made — knowing Saddam, knowing what he’d done in the past, (I had) high confidence that he was hiding and keeping (WMDs).”

Despite the appearance of normalcy, 9/11 deranged America. The Department of Homeland Security, founded during the first few months of our stay there, was a symptom of this derangement. The idea of a capitalised ‘Homeland’ should give any liberal pause: it is a way of making a country a bunker. The energy invested in combating enemies without, will, as night follows day, be redirected at enemies within. There is an umbilical connection between the founding of the Department of Homeland Security and Donald Trump’s ICE raids that saw masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents attack, kidnap, and kill not just illegals but citizens.

The Department of Homeland Security begat ICE. It was created as one of the Department’s most powerful agencies. Congress granted ICE a unique combination of civil and criminal authorities to protect national security and public safety in response to the events of 9/11. The State apparatus created by George W. Bush and Dick Cheney enabled the depredations of Donald Trump.

Just as China was entering the WTO, a step that enabled the greatest economic transformation the world has ever seen, the United States of America used the unipolar moment and 9/11 to stamp its own licence to kill. As China built, America rampaged. The one thing that this twenty-fifth commemoration brings into focus is the epoch of American violence flagged off by 9/11. In this quarter of a century, the US and its allies have attacked and tried to conquer Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Yemen, Syria, Lebanon, Iran and Palestine. This is not an exhaustive list.

Its NATO allies and its henchmen in the so-called Abraham Accords (Israel and the United Arab Emirates) have enabled such devastation, ruination and genocide that we should find a name for this broederbond that historians can handily remember. The Axis of Evil is taken; the Meridian of Malevolence, perhaps? If that doesn’t slide off the tongue, how about the Ark of Atrocity?

When Christopher Hitchens became a born-again neo-con, he wanted to invade Iraq because he yearned to be part of a revolution. Having confected a world-historical enemy — ‘Islamofascism’ — he was going to overthrow it in Iraq, with a little help from his hard-Right, deep State friends. It was a squalid end to a lively intellectual career, but he did make history of a sort. The American counter-revolution that he had a hand in enabling, grew and grew and has now, under Trump, begun devouring its children.

editorials.title: Shah, Rajnath greet Mohan Bhagwat at 76; PM Modi’s silence stands out
editorials.passage:
The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh chief, Mohan Bhagwat, turned 76 on Friday, receiving birthday greetings from several senior Bharatiya Janata Party leaders, including the Union ministers, Amit Shah and Rajnath Singh. But one conspicuous omission stood out: Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not publicly greet the RSS chief. Shah hailed Bhagwat’s journey from a sangh pracharak to sarsanghchalak as an unparalleled example of “dedication to national service, social harmony and preservation and promotion of Indian culture”. Singh said Bhagwat had devoted his life to strengthening national unity and integrity, fostering social harmony and preserving Indian culture and values. Modi’s silence was particularly striking given the warmth of his response last year, when Bhagwat turned 75. Modi had written newspaper articles and posted them on X, praising the RSS chief for dedicating his life to “societal transformation” and strengthening harmony and fraternity. On Friday, while still occupied with the BRICS Summit, Modi posted about the anniversary of Swami Vivekananda’s historic Chicago speech. But there was nothing for Bhagwat. It was not clear whether Modi had called him privately. The two leaders are contemporaries, with Modi turning 76 on September 17. The RSS, however, has no tradition of celebrating birthdays and neither Bhagwat nor other senior sangh leaders greet Modi publicly on his birthday.

The chief minister of Karnataka, DK Shivakumar, completed 100 days in office this week. But the anniversary has not been a happy one. At first, the planning and statistics minister, B Nagendra, was forced to quit over allegations of involvement in the embezzlement of funds from Karnataka Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation Ltd. In yet another controversy surrounding Shivakumar’s cabinet colleagues, the Enforcement Directorate raided the house of the Karnataka public works department minister, Satish Jarkiholi. The raid unearthed documents pertaining to his stakes in an African gold-mining company in Congo and revealed that the foreign assets were acquired using bribes for PWD tenders. The Central agency claimed that it had seized Rs 3.3 crore of unaccounted-for cash and foreign currency in dollars and euros amounting to Rs 15 lakh. It is alleged that his parliamentarian daughter, Priyanka Jarkiholi, and son, Rahul Jarkiholi, among other family members, including his two brothers who are legislators, and a horde of his aides have also got stakes in foreign investment and unaccounted-for cash. Curiously, Satish claimed that the scheduled tribe community is upset over the ED raids.

Politicians jumped at the 1980s trend on ChatGPT, posting images of themselves in attire and poses associated with pop culture of that decade. But things turned serious with the Congress’s Kerala handle posting a picture of an Amit Shah-like man in a Maruti Omni — a van associated with kidnapping in cinema of the 1980s and 1990s — with the caption “a Gujarat street in the 80s”. The Gujarat BJP responded with an image of the former PM, Rajiv Gandhi, in an Omni covered in blood and filled with Congress supporters with sticks, alluding to the 1984 Sikh pogrom in the capital. Several BJP handles also posted AI-images with a likeness of Sonia Gandhi as a bartender or bar dancer, prompting the Congressman, Gaurav Pandhi, to point out that the expelled Jana Sangh leader, Balraj Madhok, wrote in his biography that the office was a “den of immoral activities”. The Jana Sangh is the predecessor of the BJP.

In 2022, an IAS couple emptied a sports stadium in Delhi to walk their dog. This incident is back in the spotlight after the Satya Niketan building collapse. The husband, Sanjeev Khirwar, is the commissioner of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi. Khirwar and his wife, Rinku Dhugga, were then transferred to Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh, respectively. But Khirwar returned to Delhi in January this year when the city was struggling with the stray dog controversy. When the Satya Niketan tragedy occurred, old stories of the controversy resurfaced. Coincidentally, his wife’s case also reached the Supreme Court. Dhugga was served compulsory retirement by the department of personnel and training on August 7, 2023, an order which she challenged in the Central Administrative Tribunal and received a favourable verdict. Now, that order is under challenge in the Supreme Court.

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: The rush for the new iPhone Duo is unconscionable
editorials.passage:
Sir — The rush for the new iPhone Duo — the price starts at a staggering Rs 2,99,900 in India while the top-end variant costs Rs 4,49,900 — is unconscionable. Here is a list of things that can be bought at that price range. The price of one top-end iPhone Duo could put school supplies in the hands of more than 800 children, provide a month’s basic ration to nearly 600 struggling households, or purchase over 4,700 children’s books. This is not all. Even if one were to spend the money on oneself, this astronomical sum could easily buy 600-700 averagely priced books. If this does not shame people, nothing will.

Aditya Mukherjee, Calcutta

Sir — As the BRICS chair in 2026, India carries considerable diplomatic responsibility. Xi Jinping, the Chinese president, is visiting India for the first time since the Galwan clash, creating an opportunity to repair strained ties between the two nations. On the other hand, it is unfortunate that the Bangladeshi prime minister, Tarique Rahman, has declined New Delhi’s invitation to attend the outreach session as BIMSTEC chair. The two-day gathering should reinforce the Global South’s voice, encourage constructive engagement, and produce tangible benefits for every participant.

Sir — Any meeting between the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, and Xi Jinping must prioritise peace along the Line of Actual Control, military de-escalation, trade deficit and market access. India should make warmer relations conditional on respect for its territorial integrity. The BRICS Summit offers Modi an added leverage: a collective commitment to sovereignty, non-coercion and stable supply chains could influence China more effectively than bilateral engagement alone. New Delhi should maintain communication with Beijing while improving border infrastructure, defence preparedness, and economic diversification. Cooperation must not weaken national security.

Sir — India’s strategic balance was evident in Narendra Modi’s meeting with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, before the BRICS Summit. Their discussions combined advocacy of peaceful negotiations with closer engagement in commerce, energy, defence and technology. The India-Russia relationship remains important to the economic interests of both countries, particularly amid global instability and an errant United States of America. New Delhi must preserve this partnership while retaining the independence that gives its diplomacy credibility.

Sir — The headline, “PM prods Putin on peace” (Sept 12), mischaracterises India’s diplomatic role. A third country involved in conflict resolution acts as a facilitator rather than an enforcer. The ministry of external affairs said the prime minister reiterated the value of negotiation and offered India’s assistance. The verb, “prods”, introduces an unwarranted suggestion of force. A neutral nation-state cannot dictate terms to sovereign powers, especially during sensitive mediation. Journalism must convey the nuances of statecraft accurately.

Sir — The BRICS demand for reform of international developmental and financial institutions is significant (“Spotlight on IMF, World Bank”, Sept 12). Emerging economies need financial bodies that are flexible, transparent and accountable. With 11 members and 10 partner countries, BRICS can itself promote sustainable, barrier-free commerce for shared prosperity of the Global South. The New Development Bank, the bloc’s multilateral lender, can further these ambitions by financing infrastructure and supporting cooperation in the region. This should be discussed at the summit.

editorials.title: What queries reveal: Editorial on AI and the changing quest for knowledge
editorials.passage:
Socrates had warned that writing creates an illusion of wisdom because people can repeat written words without truly knowing what they mean. The warning seems to have acquired an urgency in the age of generative Artificial Intelligence. Google’s annual records of popular queries asked by its users offer a compressed account of collective anxieties and desires. People, for instance, googled to find out how wildfires start, how to register to vote, how to increase oxygen levels during Covid and, among other queries, what unfamiliar laws, diseases or internet expressions mean. The search engine has functioned principally as an index in this context: users supplied keywords, examined the links thrown up by the browser, and arrived at an answer. But a recent compilation of such queries from 2015 to 2025 by Google’s data editor, Simon Rogers, offers an illuminating perspective on a shift in humanity’s quest for knowledge. With the advent of AI and its integration into Google, questions are becoming longer, more intimate and conversational. In 2025, searches beginning with “Tell me about…” rose by 70% over the previous year, while “How do I…” queries reached an all-time high. This change may seem subtle but it records a transfer of responsibility. Users are increasingly asking Google to interpret events, compare choices, formulate arguments and provide reassurance and AI does this for them.

The rising popularity of a conversational search is understandable. It permits a fuller expression of human curiosity as complex questions can contain context, qualifications and competing priorities that a string of keywords cannot accommodate. Yet, the convenience of a synthesised response reduces the effort required to compare sources, read divergent opinions and arrive at an independent conclusion. The Pew Research Center found that users clicked on conventional links during 8% of visits when a Google AI summary appeared, compared with 15% when one was absent. AI’s conclusions are masquerading as definitive information, eliminating the process of thinking and deduction after analysing different sources. Generative AI compounds the problem because its answers remain coherent even when evidence is weak, incomplete or false. Coherence can easily be mistaken for erudition — as Socrates cautioned.

The deeper concern, though, is whether AI is redirecting human curiosity towards intellectual de­pendence. Immanuel Kant defined enlightenment as the emergence from self-incurred immaturity, a condition sustained by permitting another authority to perform the work of understanding. AI systems now offer precisely that service at unprecedented speed and scale. Another philosopher, Hannah Arendt, treated judgement as an activity requiring reflection upon different standpoints; an AI answer occludes those differences.

The barrage of the last decade’s queries to Google shows that the hu­man desire to understand and to know remains strong. But the means of understanding has changed. People now seek a decisive response without examining the contest among facts, interpretations and interests from which responsible judgement arises. Humans are sacrificing the demanding practice of enquiry at the altar of the need for immediate answers. The price for this — Socrates was right — will be the erosion of the ability to reason.

editorials.title: Editorial. Risky bets
editorials.passage:
There has been frenzied activity in the primary market for equities in the last three years — with promoters making the most of growing demand to raise capital at extremely high valuations, and investors buying these issuances to rake in quick gains. What is concerning here is that mutual funds have been participating aggressively in the primary market in recent years. A recernt analysis by this newspaper shows that mutual fund investments accounted for around one-third of the aggregate size of the mainboard IPOs in 2024 and 2025 and 26.6 per cent of the IPOs which opened between January and August 2026.

Investments in the primary market are riskier than in the secondary market due to the sheer lack of information on companies making primary offers. Information about an IPO-bound company is largely limited to its offer documents. In the case of a listed stock, there would be sufficient historical record of financial and operational performance as well as management conduct to help investors take an informed decision. With primary issues, the risk has been compounded by price manipulation in many stocks in the period immediately following the listing to enable subscribers to exit early with hefty gains. But given the pressure on mutual funds to deploy high inflows through systematic investment plans, they appear keen to invest in IPOs — often without due diligence. This could hurt investor interests.

Mutual funds invested in over 90 per cent of the IPOs between 2020 and 2022 and around 78 per cent of those over the last four years. The amount of investor funds invested in primary market has been increasing steadily; rising from ₹6,684 crore in 2020 to ₹57,668 crore in 2025. SEBI’s rules have been largely supportive of mutual fund money flowing into the primary market. The regulator allows them to invest through the qualified institutional buyer category or as anchor investors, one day prior to the opening of the IPO. Given the confirmed allocation in the anchor investor portion, mutual funds have been leaning on this route to buy IPO stocks.

But many fund managers appear to be viewing primary market investment as a short-term opportunity. According to a recent SEBI survey, MFs had exited 38 per cent of the anchor allotment by the end of one year from allotment. SEBI must review the rules governing mutual funds’ investment in primary offerings. Last year, the regulator had barred mutual funds from participating in pre-IPO placements since that could saddle them with illiquid securities, if the offer is delayed. Rules can be carved out for MF schemes which are eligible to invest in IPOs. Special primary market funds can be introduced as a category, where IPO stocks can be parked. That will also give investors the option of choosing to invest in IPO offerings. If regular equity or hybrid schemes invest in primary offerings, the value of these investments should be limited to less than 5 per cent of the portfolio value.

Published on September 11, 2026

editorials.title: Fifth column by Tavleen Singh: Who are the real patriots?
editorials.passage: There appears to be a fifth columnist in the Prime Minister’s inner circle. This thought came to me when I saw him jubilantly striding across that college stage in Vadodara last week. The event seemed part of his Gen-Z seduction crusade, and what he strode, smiled and waved to was the tune of We Will Rock You. Luckily, it was only the tune that played. Had he been aware of the words, Modi may have fainted. Here is a line: ‘You got mud on your face, big disgrace. Somebody better put you back into your place.’ See what I mean about a fifth columnist working in the innards of the PMO? Also, the song is from 1977 when people of my generation were young and rebellious, and the cockroaches who have now got so badly under Modi’s skin were not even specks on the horizon. More seriously — who was the idiot who advised the Prime Minister to attend this joyous event at a time when a PG (paying guest) hostel had just crumbled in Delhi University’s south campus, killing young students and their dreams? Among the dead was eighteen-year-old Arpit Jaj, whose taxi driver father worked overtime to send his son to college and struggled to pay the exorbitant rent for his PG hovel. I heard Arpit’s story in Barkha Dutt’s Mojo Story. It brought tears to my eyes. ALSO READFifth column by Tavleen Singh: Small dreams too important to ignore We in the mainstream media have mostly ignored the stories of the seven dead students. Perhaps because they would all be as heartbreaking. Instead, almost every news channel reported every moment of the Prime Minister’s trip to Gujarat as if it was the most important news of the day. If they had stayed with the building collapse in Satya Niketan, there may have been some hope of coercing the ‘triple-engine’ government in Delhi to stem the corruption that led to the horror of students being killed for just trying to get a college degree. While the Chief Minister’s cohort surveyed the debris of the illegally built PG (paying guest) hostel from high above, a handful of real journalists dug deeper into the crashed building and showed pictures of the horrendous conditions in which students live. The Cockroach Janta Party leader who said that students are being forced to live like cockroaches is correct. The building that crumbled is among others in which students live in cells built one upon the other, and that can only be reached through dangerously narrow alleys darkened by clumps of hanging wires. I must here add that the best reporting I saw came from a digital platform called PEEK TV. When I saw their pictures of those dismal alleyways and dreary rooms, I found myself hoping that the Prime Minister was also watching so he could understand why he needs to forget about our ‘demographic dividend’. Young students who are forced to live and study in such horrible conditions will never learn to think, dream or learn. How will they be able to compete with students who, in other colleges in other countries, have already learned how to deal with the technological revolution that AI brings? This one building collapse has brought to the surface many other things, like the abysmal state of governance in Delhi. It has revealed corruption so evil that it boggles the mind. Everyone is involved in creating the smokescreen that allows builders to disobey the rules of safe planning. The PG mafia that extorts inexplicably high rents from desperate students is controlled by politicians and high officials who always seem to get away with their evil deeds. ALSO READFifth column by Tavleen Singh: Am I a Naxal? The only thing that happens after every disaster of the kind we saw in Satya Niketan is that some lowly officials get publicly yelled at by higher officials like the Chief Minister and then some committee is appointed to (supposedly) go into causes and solutions. These committees never amount to much, as we can see from the one appointed after the building collapse in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar some months ago. Corrupt officials and politicians collude to make Delhi nonfunctional except when there is a big conference of the BRICS kind. And then things only appear to work because visiting dignitaries are only allowed to see restricted sections of India’s capital city. This is the way things are. It is the way things have always been. But the cockroaches and their young cheerleaders are ensuring this is not how they will always be in the future. It is the one thing that gives me some hope that a day will come when officials and politicians who have created the mess that we see today pay for their crimes. One idea from me is that the officials who allowed that PG hostel to be built should be charged with manslaughter, and that this be done every time a building collapses and kills people. No more committees. No more inquiry commissions. When people die because of the criminal negligence of officials, those officials should be charged with manslaughter, if not murder. Meanwhile, the Prime Minister needs to find out who the fifth columnist is in his inner circle and punish him for sending him off to college events where he blames what is wrong with India on ‘dimagi naxals’. He seems quite proud of this new label, without noticing that the people he is charging with sedition could be the very patriots that we need today .

editorials.title: Across the aisle by P Chidambaram: Holding a mirror to GDP numbers
editorials.passage: As someone said, tongue in cheek, people don’t eat GDP numbers. People eat food, wear clothes and footwear, send their children to school, buy medicines, use mobile phones, watch television, scroll social media, and want to be safe and happy — measured as Consumption. The aggregate of Consumption (C), Investment (I), Government spending (G) and net Exports (X -M) — after factoring for taxes and subsidies— is Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Measurement of GDP, especially the rate of growth of GDP, is crucial to gauge the health of the economy. Healthier debate The MoSPI has released the GDP numbers for Q1 of 2026-27: the rate of growth is 10.3% in nominal (current) prices and 7.8 per cent in constant prices compared to Q1 2025-26. The government and the sarkari economists are pleased. The sceptics have raised questions. There is a raging debate on the credibility of the GDP numbers. Rather than debating the desirability of ‘one nation, one election’ (which will undermine federal parliamentary democracy), it is better to debate the GDP numbers and whether the benefits of growth are percolating to the people. I do not wish to add to the noise. Let’s assume that MoSPI’s numbers are correct. My calculations of the compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of nominal and real GDP on two different base years are (see Table): Notably, on the old base year and the new base year, the CAGR beginning 2022-23 is more or less the same. The growth rate in Q1 of 2026-27 is only marginally higher. Conclusion: the economy has not shifted gears in 2026-27; nor is it in overdrive. Therefore, no boast is warranted. ALSO READIndia’s Q1 GDP growth hits 7.8%, beats RBI forecast and market expectations Pertinent questions Let’s hold a mirror to the latest GDP numbers. The nagging question is, under the old base year, the GDP in constant prices is very depressed compared to the GDP in current prices but it is not so under the new base year. Why? Be that as it may, the growth rate ought to be reflected in the measurable parameters of the economy such as jobs, wages, consumption, trade, investment, etc. Here are some pertinent questions: Why is the unemployment rate among youth of 15-29 years at a high of 16.2 per cent? CMIE has reported that the unemployment rate for graduates aged 29-34 years often touches 40-45 per cent; why? According to NITI Aayog, 8.7 crore youth aged 15-29 are ‘Not in Employment, Education or Training’ (NEET); why?  Why are real wages growing at dismal rates of (-) 5.5, 1.7 and 3.3 per cent, respectively, among casual, salaried and self-employed workers? (source: PLFS). Twenty per cent of the workforce is casual labour and will they not be further impoverished by the negative wage growth?  Why is net FDI so low? FCNR (B) mobilization which carried interest rates of 6-7 per cent came in truckloads, but why is foreign capital not coming as direct investment?  When forex reserves have touched an all-time high of USD 740 billion, why has the rupee not appreciated? Since January 2026, the rupee has depreciated nearly 5 per cent against the US dollar and is reportedly the worst performing Asian currency; why?  Exports are rising, but imports are rising too. At current prices, imports are rising faster. Merchandise trade deficit touched USD 150 billion in April-August 2026. The trade deficit with China alone in April-July was USD 44 billion. Is the trade deficit not a drag on the economy? Why are Make-in-India, PLI, ASPIRE, NMCP and other schemes not resulting in manufacture of the goods that India imports from China?  In the sectoral composition of nominal GVA, why is ‘manufacturing’ stagnant at 13 per cent? In fact, the share of the secondary sector in nominal GVA, over many quarters, has been bound between 24 and 26 per cent. Why have the schemes not pushed up the needle?  Why is capital investment, as measured by Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF), stuck at roughly 33.5 per cent of GDP? Of this, private corporate capital expenditure has remained unchanged at about 12 per cent. Despite cajolery, admonishments and threats, why are corporate investors not willing to make capital investment?  Why has the growth number not resulted in more public goods such as better schools, better hospitals, better roads, better water supply, better policing, etc.? If one takes a straw poll, the overwhelming proportion of citizens will give a thumbs down on each of these areas. ALSO READExplainer: Why double deflation matters for measuring real growth Unedifying mirror image There is no surprise that Gen Z is protesting against the marked deterioration all around them. We may be growing at 7.8 per cent statistically, but most citizens do not feel or believe so. Because they know that their lives are not better or easier.

editorials.title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in
editorials.passage:
U kraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs , pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.

Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan . Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties , his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff , back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.

This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?

The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022, then left them to sink or swim . Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors and paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’s nauseating Alaska summit , and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.

Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About 60% oppose ceding Donbas land to Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians also want it to stop . And like Moscow, Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch , notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly a deal to be done . But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.

Efforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has now extended to the Red Sea (Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modern forever war phenomenon . Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but to win a Nobel peace prize (plus lucrative Russian energy deals).

Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas. Trump’s “board of peace” and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fear fighting will drag on indefinitely . Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.

Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led to war crime atrocities such as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedly killed more than 100 schoolgirls in February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.

Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightly restricted international journalists’ access to Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost of successful Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.

Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.

Western democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly, urged here ) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator
