editorials.title: Warning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still can
editorials.passage:
I magine this. Quite by chance, your TikTok feed presents you with footage of the fascists who recently took part in highly organised shows of strength in Dover and Portsmouth (and, on Wednesday, outside the London offices of the Daily Mail , demanding a new house for the mother of their leader, Daniel “Tommo” Thomas). For as long as the images hold your attention, you see and hear flashes of explanation, but then, as usual, you scroll away to someone leaping off a tall building, a fight on the London Underground, or a trick-performing dog.

Hypothetically, TikTok users are able to skip through 260 videos in under 35 minutes . And it’s this distracted, quick-fire way that so many people receive information that may be responsible for a worrying statistic from YouGov last week . Its poll on the Dover and Portsmouth events showed that 53% of people aged 18-24 years old simply didn’t have a point of view on whether the masked demonstrations were “a legitimate way of protesting”. Further, 43% of those of all ages were either unaware of the story, or not following it at all.

Those figures probably highlight one of the most worrying aspects of the times we live in: the decline of reading. Millions of us know what that phenomenon feels like: trying desperately to keep your attention glued to a book or news article with the nagging certainty that you will be tempted back to the more ephemeral attractions offered by your phone. But a background in the pre-digital world helps people not just follow national and global events, but clarify and contextualise them. In this case, at the risk of sounding hopelessly pompous, the fear many of us felt as we watched what happened in both ports was surely full of the perspectives gleaned from years of soaking up books and newspapers – and the sense that history often either repeats itself, or rhymes.

Black-clad – let’s be honest: uniformed – men who want to “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British”, while claiming to be protecting women and girls: the whole spectacle was pitched halfway between Oswald Moseley’s blackshirts – and, therefore, Hitler and the Nazis – and the Ku Klux Klan, with the seemingly ubiquitous balaclavas lacing everything with a flavour of the Troubles. But if you receive most of your information in the form of a distracting and seemingly infinite jumble of random moving images, what would you know about most of that?

All this crossed my mind thanks to an excellent new book marking what may well be a transformative moment for societies all over the world. The New Dark Ages is the work of the Times columnist James Marriott, and subtitled The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society. Presumably to accommodate itself to the changes it describes, it is short: 208 pages. But it is also full of insight and urgency.

In the 20 years since the UK’s National Literacy Trust began looking at children’s and young people’s reading, there has been a 36% fall in the number who say they enjoy reading in their spare time, to its lowest level on record. In 2024, the Guardian reported a survey by the Reading Agency charity , which found that 35% of adults said they were now “lapsed readers”, meaning that they used to regularly read for pleasure, but “rarely or never” did any more.

The Atlantic magazine recently ran an article baldly headlined The End of Reading Is Here , whose author, Rose Horowitch, made plenty of sobering claims. “The literate era will prove to be a brief interlude between the oral and digital ages,” she wrote – and drew on no end of evidence and anecdotes. A program director at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, for instance, ran focus groups asking high-school students about recreational reading. The conclusion: “most thought of it as an alien practice”. When Marriott first wrote about this, he says, “some professors reported that it was not that the young men and women in their classes were unwilling to read, but that they seemed almost unable to”.

In Britain, more than 320 newspapers closed down between 2009 and 2019 , a statistic the book follows with a stark suggestion: “It is increasingly possible to get through life without any exposure to the news at all.” In the wake of the 2016 Brexit referendum, I met people who said they had simply stopped paying attention to current affairs because they were so maddening: now, I wonder if what was really powering this switch-off was technology. The resulting ignorance – a strong word, but it feels justified – is firewalled by phone screens: it feels as if the only stuff that can break through has to be angry, paranoid and visually shocking.

And because of the decline of reading, the people who purvey all the nonsense and poison can be increasingly confident that fewer and fewer people will come across anything halfway critical or analytical. In that sense, the screen age is exemplified by – oh yes – Donald Trump, who, according to an economic adviser in his first term, “won’t read anything – not one-page memos, not the brief policy papers, nothing”. His style of speechmaking is equally non-literate: as Marriott writes, “he doesn’t supply evidence for his ideas. Rather than organising his information analytically via clauses and subclauses in the manner of literate communication, he merely piles up assertions”.

His proposed election bribe of $5,000 is one surreal example, but there are plenty of others. I recently watched an online video of Sean Duffy , the former Fox Business host who is now Trump’s secretary of transportation. He was rejoicing in the administration’s quest to do away with start-stop ignition buttons in cars – mainly, I sensed, because of some weird quasi-Freudian attachment to the phallic(ish) shape of traditional keys. Written down in an attempt at coherent argument, his case would have looked ridiculous. But folksily barked out as Duffy’s “pet peeve”, I could imagine it being warmly greeted by exactly the people it was aimed at. The same, of course, applies to any number of much more malignant Trumpian positions and passions: climate denial, brazen racism towards Somali-Americans, unapologetic Islamophobia and the idea that the US is about to be overrun by criminals and the occupants of other countries’ prisons and mental institutions.

“Mass literacy is a recent phenomenon,” Marriott writes. “So is mass democracy. We simply don’t know whether one can survive without the other.” Meanwhile, on millions of screens, fascist faux-militias, populists and other merchants of loathing and absurdity blur into acrobatic skateboarders, arguments on the tube and dogs that do tricks. That strips them of context and thereby normalises their rise – and inch by inch, we move towards a future with echoes of the past that too many people will have failed to understand. And this time, there will be no books to burn, because we will have stopped reading them.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: As Australia faces an AI-generated future, a human rights act is needed more than ever
editorials.passage:
As we hurtle towards a post-human future, the absence of a human rights act in Australia will put us all at ever greater risk.

Human rights, which the Australian parliament has never managed to properly legislate despite overwhelming public support, risks becoming a dimly remembered artefact of another age at precisely the moment we need it most.

Artificial – authoritarian – intelligence, automated decision-making, independent assessment tools and algorithms will shape the lives we live and the public support we receive.

But human rights are not adequately legislated in Canberra – despite the recommendation of a parliamentary committee , a huge petition and campaign and effective laws in Victoria, Queensland and ACT. Now rights can easily be lost in an environment shaped by opaque algorithms and computers that say no.

The government has been patting itself on the back with its proposed digital duty of care – “my feed my way”, as the prime minister announced with uncharacteristic pithiness. It aims to introduce limits on the algorithms perfected by the global surveillance giants and give Australians the right to help shape the information they receive (but not its accuracy).

Meanwhile, the government is racing to use similar tools to that determine how much support people receive for essential services when they need them most. Kate Chaney’s private member’s bill is the only sign of pushback.

Hundreds of thousands of public servants have been trained on how to use artificial intelligence. Yet the information commissioner found that few departments declared their use of AI.

GovAI is set to become something more than an announcement. Every department and agency was required to appoint a chief AI officer by July.

Come December, the privacy statements of every department – and company – that uses AI to make decisions that impact human beings will have to be updated to note this.

But who reads privacy statements before clicking consent?

The law falls short of the robodebt royal commission recommendations. It does not require companies and departments to reveal how the process works, the business rules and algorithms, or provide a right to human review of automated decisions.

The provision of care to older Australians is currently the biggest canary in this mine.

After only 10 months, it is clear that the department of ageing’s automated integrated assessment tool (IAT) – used to determine eligibility and access to services – is failing. Contrary to all best practise recommendations or the scarifying experience of robodebt, it has no human oversight or override options.

As Melissa Davey reported , within days of the tool’s adoption, alarm bells began to ring.

State health officials recognised that it was potentially catastrophic; spreadsheets of inappropriate decisions were compiled in every state. “Misaligned IAT outcomes”, they were called in NSW. In the words of the head of WA Health: “Without a pathway for discretion, a small but vulnerable group of older people might experience catastrophic outcomes while waiting for algorithmically determined access to services.”

Beyond the human pain and suffering, this matters a great deal for the states and territories. It is their hospital beds that become the only option for elderly people who cannot get adequate care at home, or access to a residential care bed.

The equivalent of whole hospitals are filled with people who should be receiving more appropriate care elsewhere.

For years we watched and listened to the horror stories of aged care as they were revealed to the royal commission. Before the commission finally reported, the pandemic exacerbated the problem as residential facilities became “no-go zones”, leaving the elderly marooned, their loved ones tapping on windows and staff fearful.

The human rights of thousands of people were gravely infringed.

Those designing the new Aged Care Act, which came into effect last November, took this seriously. The beginning of the act is a testament to the fundamental right to be treated with dignity, respect and independence.

In residential care homes all over Australia, the statement of the human rights of the elder person was tacked up on notice boards for those who could still read – and their loved ones – to note.

What was not so prominent was the inability of those residents to take legal action if their rights were breached. There was a complaints mechanism, but these were not fully legally enforceable rights .

The human right of the aged to care were again to be rationed – by algorithms, queues for assessments, caps on the number of places and access to providers, by regulations that made delivering services at home or in facilities onerous.

At the time, it was only the super-observant departmental officials in the states and some advocacy groups who realised access was also being rationed by an algorithm that could not be overridden by a human being.

The contrast between the frontend of the Aged Care Act and its backend implementation could not have been sharper. The beginning of the act describes the rights of older Australians to receive care and be treated with dignity and respect. But the implementation is about transactions: minutes of care, checklists of tasks, organisational obligations.

“The plumbing of the reforms is undermining the poetry of the act,” the former inspector general of aged care Natalie Siegel-Brown told the National Press Club .

Instead of life, it is the human rights of the elderly, that to paraphrase TS Eliot , are being “measured out … with coffee spoons”.

Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of Australia

editorials.title: Think of the parable of a frog in boiling water. That’s us dithering as the ‘unprecedented‘ weather becomes more extreme
editorials.passage:
R ecently, I overheard a conversation in a cafe where someone described their toast as “awesome”. I felt myself bristle. Not because the toast wasn’t good – I didn’t taste it – but because I remember a time when “awesome” meant something that inspired awe: towering mountains, the vastness of the night sky, the haunting song of a humpback whale. Now it’s being used to describe breakfast.

“Fantastic” has met the same fate, shedding its fantastical origins to become a synonym for “great”. Meanwhile “literally” has been so thoroughly abused that it can now mean something that is, quite literally, not literal.

Linguists call this “semantic bleaching”: the gradual erosion of a word’s original meaning through overuse. Which got me thinking about another word we hear with increasing frequency: “unprecedented”, the go-to adjective in reporting about the climate crisis. In recent months, I’ve read about unprecedented heat , unprecedented rain , unprecedented drought and unprecedented wildfires . Batten down the hatches: reports suggest that the current El Niño is going to be – you guessed it – unprecedented .

The dictionary definition hasn’t changed. “Unprecedented” still means something that has never happened before – and all the events described above have indeed represented a ratcheting up of the severity of heat, drought, rain and fire. But the word is being used so often, it feels as though it’s losing its punch. The extraordinary is starting to sound ordinary, the unprecedented almost routine.

And yet, there is nothing ordinary about what is happening. Britain has just experienced its hottest summer on record , beating the previous record set only last year. When climate-related records keep being smashed , it raises a question: what do we actually find remarkable?

In a study analysing more than 2bn weather-related social-media posts , Frances Moore from the University of California, Davis, and colleagues found that when it comes to temperature, remarkability changes with repeated exposure. Unprecedented temperatures feel less remarkable when we’ve experienced similar ones in the previous few years. We don’t make judgments based on historical precedents or childhood memories, but on what we’ve lived through recently. In other words, something can be historically unprecedented but psychologically precedented.

This means our yardstick for what counts as normal or remarkable is constantly changing. Ecologists call this “shifting baseline syndrome”. This was originally described in the context of fisheries, when Daniel Pauly noted that successive generations of fisheries scientists accepted increasingly depleted fish populations as their baseline. We now realise that the phenomenon is widespread , applying not just to biodiversity loss, but to pollution, environmental degradation and the climate crisis.

But Moore’s study contained a twist. Although extreme temperatures became less remarkable with repeated exposure, the negative feelings they provoked didn’t fade. We may stop finding unprecedented temperatures remarkable, but that doesn’t mean we find them tolerable. We’re not necessarily becoming blase about the climate crisis. We can still recognise that something is unpleasant without realising how unusual it is.

You have probably heard the parable of the boiling frog . When the unfortunate amphibian is placed in a pot of slowly warming water, it supposedly fails to notice the gradual rise in temperature and stays put until it croaks. So, here we all are, bobbing around in our family-size Le Creusets, marvelling at how balmy the water feels, as we complain that we’re starting to poach.

And that’s the dangerous bit. If extreme temperatures become familiar, we may be less likely to recognise just how extraordinary they are. What once would have seemed remarkable becomes just another hot summer, another flooded street, another crop failure. The baseline shifts, and with it our sense of what needs fixing. If the water feels normal, we may be less likely to demand that the heat be turned down.

Which brings us back to the frog. As it turns out, the old parable gets it completely wrong. No healthy frog would sit idly in a warming pan of water. They feel the heat and respond to it. When the temperature crosses a threshold, they hop out. So, maybe that’s the question we should be asking ourselves. If we can no longer recognise how remarkable these uncomfortable temperatures are, what will it take for us to do what the frog does: respond to the heat?

One place to start is with the words we use to describe what is happening. “Awesome” became ordinary because we kept using it for ordinary things – such as warm bread and marmalade. Climate extremes are different: the events themselves haven’t become ordinary, even if our experience of them is becoming more familiar. “Unprecedented” is in danger of becoming a synonym for “really extreme”. It shouldn’t. The word tells us that we have crossed into territory humanity has never experienced before. It’s important we retain that historical meaning.

Perhaps one of the most unsettling things about a heating world is not that unprecedented weather keeps happening. It’s that “unprecedented” is beginning to sound like a perfectly normal thing to say.

Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects

editorials.title: The far right is becoming normalised in Germany – and winning. Australia should take heed
editorials.passage:
The recent win for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Germany is shocking, except it’s not shocking. The writing has been on the wall for quite some time.

Last Sunday, the far-right, pro-Russian and anti-immigration AfD won almost 44% of the vote in the election in Saxony-Anhalt, a largely rural state in the former East Germany, more than doubling its previous result and finishing far ahead of the Christian Democrats.

It sits within a troubling global trend. In 2025, nearly one in four countries worldwide experienced democratic backsliding , with Europe and North America home to six of the 10 countries newly identified as autocratising, including Italy, the UK and the US.

Despite the cultural and historical differences, Australia is not immune. We cannot afford to be complacent.

This time last year, I travelled to Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a predominantly rural region in Germany’s north-east, to examine the culture of the far right and its counter-responses as part of my research. Like Saxony-Anhalt, it’s an area where the AfD has significant support. My colleagues and I spent days walking the streets of towns and cities, including Rostock and Greifswald, as well as attending an anti-fascist music festival. We wanted to understand how extremism was encountered and expressed in everyday life. But what we found, or more precisely did not find, surprised us.

For a politics so extreme and increasingly popular, visual expressions of the far right were remarkably scarce. We encountered graffitied walls and hundreds of activist stickers on street signs, lamp-posts and electricity boxes. Of these, only one or two were associated with the far right. The counter-movement dominated the streetscape. Its stickers and graffiti were vibrant, loud and sharp, with a clear intent and recurring “anti-fascist” message. Yet a subtler pattern was emerging. The far right was made visible not through its own stickers or graffiti, but in the intolerance directed towards the counter-movement: freshly placed anti-fascist and pro-refugee stickers were being actively defaced.

Looking back now, that landscape feels strangely prescient. As far-right ideas move beyond the fringe and enter mainstream political discourse, they become harder to detect, let alone recognise as extreme – an insidious process that gradually reshapes what is considered “normal”.

In Australia, we tend to imagine the far right as young white men dressed in black and wearing balaclavas, marching through the streets, performing Nazi salutes or standing in front of historic buildings holding banners. These deliberate acts of spectacle are designed to attract attention, provoke and intimidate. They are easy to identify and condemn, appearing separate from the political mainstream.

But far-right politics does not only appear wearing a balaclava. Increasingly, it does not look extreme at all. Across Europe, far-right politicians are neat, polished and smooth-talking. They are unnervingly normal . Their messages are often simple and repeatable, circulating like memes through algorithm-driven news feeds, amplified by increasingly powerful actors in the tech and media sectors and, in some cases, legitimised at the ballot box.

While One Nation politicians are a long way from the smooth-talking politicians we see in the AfD, the minor party’s recent successes in byelections in Farrer and Secret Harbour should make us take notice.

AfD and One Nation may not look or even sound the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet. Their histories, politics and contexts are different, but both draw on exclusion, national restoration, grievance and distrust. Their growing electoral success raises a critical question: why are these ideas finding a more receptive audience now?

Part of the answer may lie in how the future is imagined. Climate disruption is intensifying amid economic insecurity, war and displacement. AI is transforming how we work, communicate and understand what is real, while immense wealth and technological power are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few. These are real, present-day challenges, and the anxiety surrounding them is being amplified through social media feeds in which extreme, frightening and divisive versions of events can dominate. At a time when the future feels increasingly uncertain, rightwing populist politics offers something simple and seductive: certainty, belonging and the promise of a return to an imagined past.

As these pressures compound, their impacts radiate through our economies, communities and politics. Instead of looking sideways for someone to blame, we need to think more critically: to question where power is held, who benefits from the decisions being made, and who is being asked to bear their consequences. Otherwise, legitimate fears about the future can too easily be used to turn people against each other.

Dr Charlotte Feakins is a heritage researcher and lecturer at the University of Sydney and co-convener of an upcoming symposium on why the humanities matter in uncertain times

editorials.title: Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact?
editorials.passage:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have captured Mocha port and now threaten to control the main waterway of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. They have also attacked several cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding about 70 people, including women and children.

The repeated attacks against Saudi energy, civil, and defence facilities, combined with the maritime blockage by Iran and its Yemeni partner the Houthis, directly raise the question of the Mecca Pact’s operationalisation between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan.

The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia can activate the mutual defence agreement. If that happens, what could a Pakistani and Turkish intervention look like?

The answer to this question necessitates some crucial background first.

The US – the main security partner of the Gulf states – has signalled for a while now that it expects regional countries to take primary responsibility for their own defence and deterrence, with US help remaining critical but limited.

That posture is already visible on the ground. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the US has not been able to provide comprehensive defence for its regional partners. On several occasions, it has even failed to stop attacks on its own bases in the Gulf.

With US presence receding and Washington emphasising regional burden-sharing, Gulf states have had to look into a new defence architecture. In September 2025, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed their first mutual defence agreement, which expanded in August this year to include Turkiye and became the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.

The three countries have since established a joint secretariat, with its headquarters in Riyadh, with Pakistan taking the chairmanship for an initial three-year term.

The pact remains in a gestation period. It does not publicly identify the thresholds or scenarios under which a member would move to direct military intervention. Its organisational and institutional structure, including rules of engagement, mechanisms of consultation, and collective defence and deterrence, are yet to be formally developed.

Now, back to the question of how the pact will be operational if a member state is attacked.

Earlier this week, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that an unprovoked aggression against Saudi Arabia, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into the kingdom, would make the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement operational, adding that “there should be no doubt in this.”

Asif, however, did not share specific details on what shape that operationalisation would take. Last month, Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan clarified that the Mecca Pact would work the same way as NATO: If a member state is attacked, it must actively request and define the specific type of help it needs.

NATO’s Article 4 allows for a member to call alliance consultations and exchange of information. Article 5 requires mutual assistance from allies, but it leaves each state to decide the nature of that assistance.

In 2012, after Syria shot down a Turkish warplane, Ankara invoked Article 4 for consultation and requested specific defence assistance. Instead of demanding direct military intervention, the Turkish government explicitly asked for Patriot missile defence batteries. NATO approved the request and deployed the systems to protect Turkish airspace.

In this context, if the Mecca Pact is to be operationalised, it would have to be Saudi Arabia that defines the type of military assistance and involvement that it needs. If, for example, Riyadh makes an actual request for Pakistani direct military intervention, beyond materiel and intelligence support, Islamabad would be obliged to comply. But the request, and the scale of the response, would still likely need to be defined and agreed in a consultation meeting.

For now, none of this has been tested as Riyadh has not invoked the pact with either Pakistan or Turkiye.

In the meantime, diplomatic efforts have intensified, with Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud talking to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

Islamabad has also publicly urged Iran to rein in the Houthis from attacking Saudi Arabia and threatening the Bab al-Mandeb, and has reminded Tehran of Pakistan’s commitment to Riyadh’s defence through the pact. Ankara would likely play its own part in diplomatically restraining the Houthis and Iran.

If diplomacy fails and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia or the Bab al-Mandeb continue, Turkiye and Pakistan would likely expand the air and technological support they already provide. Islamabad already has an air squadron of about 16 JF-17 Thunder multirole aircraft, defence systems, and thousands of troops deployed in Saudi Arabia.

But a direct military operation by Pakistani forces inside Yemen remains unlikely at the moment. Given the disastrous and lasting impacts of its participation in the Afghan war against the Soviet Union on behalf of the US, Pakistan would be far more wary of joining a war against Iran and its allies, for fear of spillover into its western border provinces’ economy, domestic security, sectarian balance, and societal harmony. Pakistani leaders would find it hard to build domestic consensus for direct attacks on the Houthis or a fight with Iran.

The likely scenario is that Pakistan would increase joint diplomatic pressure on Iran to restrain the Houthis, further augment its support for Saudi defence, and push for a multinational naval coalition to secure the Bab al-Mandeb. Adopting this restraint would still keep the essence of the Mecca Pact intact, while putting more weight behind regional de-escalation.

The new security architecture that agreements like the Mecca Pact are setting up will take years to mature. Until the mechanisms and rules of collective response develop, Pakistan’s existing bilateral defence relationships with Saudi Arabia and other Arab partners will continue to focus on defence needs.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Science can be the bridge between India and China that diplomacy could not build
editorials.passage:
I n the second half of the 5th century, two mathematicians living over 3000 km apart were working on the same fundamental number that relates the circumference of a circle to its radius. In southern China around 480 CE, the astronomer Zu Chongzhi estimated the value of π to be between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927. Writing in 499 CE at Kusumapura (modern day Patna), the Indian astronomer Aryabhata independently arrived at 3.1416. Neither scholar had ever heard of the other. These estimates reigned for a thousand years, until Madhava in Kerala and Jamshid Al-Kashi in Samarkand improved on them around the turn of the 15th century. This historical convergence makes a philosophical point before it makes a historical one. The number π does not belong to any particular civilisation. It is neither Chinese nor Indian. Two distinct traditions converged on the same mathematical truth because the truth was there uniquely to be found. This is distinctive of science among human undertakings: it is arguably the only intellectual enterprise where independent efforts applied to reality, arrive at the same destination. Literature does not do this. History does not do this. Even Law does not do this. Only mathematics and the natural sciences do. That peculiarity has implications for how rival geopolitical powers should approach science. The Tang court worked this out long before Delhi or Beijing had cause to think about it again.

That peculiarity has implications for how rival geopolitical powers should approach science. The Tang court worked this out long before Delhi or Beijing had cause to think about it again.

A lesson in pragmatism from the Tang Court In 718 CE Gautama Siddha, an astronomer of Indian descent born in Chang’an, translated the Indian Navagraha calendar into Chinese at the throne’s request, bringing with it Indian numerals, the zero, and a table of sines. Eleven years later a Tang meridian survey stretching from northern Vietnam to the steppe produced the Dayan calendar, formulated by the monk-astronomer Yixing. In 733 CE Gautama Siddha’s son, Gautama Zhuan, formally accused the recently deceased Yixing of plagiarising the Indian work, a charge tied to his own family’s prestige and position. The Tang court did not settle the matter by deciding whose civilisation deserved the credit. It investigated, and found the charge false: the dynastic history records that it sprang from Gautama Zhuan’s resentment at being excluded from the reform, not from any fault in Yixing’s calculations. Historians still debate how much Yixing owed to Indian sources; his use of the tangent almost certainly did. But the court cleared him of copying. The point is that a dispute from 1300 years ago is settled the way historians of science still settle disputes today — by returning to the calculations rather than asking which side one would prefer to be right. It is our argument for engagement between two states that will remain competitors on nearly every other axis. Diplomacy manages disagreement. Law adjudicates it. Science can dissolve it, because a well-posed question about the physical world has an answer that does not care who is asking. Also read: The real BRICS story is what China, Russia want & India wishes The BRICS 2026: Operationalising rhetoric Chinese President Xi Jinping is in New Delhi for the 18th BRICS Summit under India’s chairship with the theme: Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. This is his first visit to India in seven years. At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last August, Prime Minister Narendra Modi told him that the interests of 2.8 billion people were bound up with cooperation between their countries which would pave the way for the welfare of all humanity. Xi reciprocated by calling both nations members of the Global South with a shared responsibility to advance human progress. Taking the leaders at their word presents an opportunity to make them come true – that does not need either government to negotiate complex treaties, legislate new frameworks, or even trust each other to honour commitments. The mechanism is simple: point two advanced scientific instruments, two distinct datasets, or two independent research groups at the same unresolved physical question, and let the question perform the unifying work that traditional diplomacy cannot. This requires looking at what already exists, built and paid for independently by two countries that were not primarily thinking of each other when they laid the foundations. Cosmic arithmetic: FAST and the uGMRT In June 2023, radio astronomical pulsar timing arrays around the world announced the first evidence for a background of gravitational waves with periods of years, the probable signature of supermassive black holes spiralling towards each other across the Universe. The Indian Pulsar Timing Array (InPTA) uses the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) near Pune, and they reported findings jointly with their European partners. China’s Pulsar Timing array (CPTA) uses the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) in Guizhou, the largest single radio dish on Earth, and they reported its findings independently. The two instruments are not duplicates. FAST achieves excellent timing precision on individual millisecond pulsars by virtue of its sheer scale and raw sensitivity. The uGMRT, however, is uniquely capable of observing at much lower radio frequencies (300–500 MHz), where the smearing effect of interstellar plasma, known as the dispersion measure, can be carefully quantified and accounted for. The dynamic nature of the interstellar medium introduces slowly varying time delays in the measured time-of-arrival of pulsar signals, which can mimic or obscure the delays introduced by passing gravitational waves. FAST’s higher-frequency observations cannot easily determine this dispersion measure correction on its own. Put the two datasets together and the measurement gets sharper in a way that neither telescope can achieve alone, just as Zu Chongzhi’s and Aryabhata’s estimates of π were each less useful than the interval they jointly defined. This is not a diplomatic nicety. It is how Nature works: two independent measurements of the same signal reduce the uncertainty on its value in a way neither measurement can on its own. The whole is indeed greater than the sum of its parts. Subterranean synergies: Neutrinos in Jiangmen and Theni A similar dynamic exists in fundamental particle physics. In 2012 the Daya Bay Reactor Neutrino experiment in China, led by physicist Yifang Wang, measured the last unknown mixing angle (θ₁₃) which determines how different flavours of neutrinos transmute through quantum mechanics into each other as they travel through space. Building on this achievement, China’s Institute of High Energy Physics then constructed the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20,000-tonne liquid scintillator detector located 700 m underground and 53 km from the Taishan and Yangjiang nuclear power plants – a distance optimised for maximum sensitivity. JUNO began taking data recently, and involves over 700 scientists from 74 institutions across 17 countries and regions. Noticeably absent from this collaboration is India which for many years has planned its own underground neutrino laboratory, the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO), in the Bodi West Hills of Theni, Tamil Nadu. INO was designed to house a 50,000-tonne magnetised Iron Calorimeter (ICAL) to study atmospheric neutrinos. Its primary scientific objective, to determine whether the third neutrino mass state is heavier or lighter than the other two, is the same objective JUNO now pursues. But the INO project was stalled indefinitely amid baseless environmental litigation and protests instigated by local politicians, leaving a generation of trained Indian particle physicists without a domestic experiment to work on. This is not an argument for political lobbying or for forcing an unnatural partnership. It is simply to emphasise a stark misalignment of resources. Decades of human expertise, built at real financial cost over many years in India, sits geographically adjacent to a Chinese experiment built to use exactly that calibre of expertise. The wall separating the physicists in Theni from the data in Jiangmen is entirely of human construction. In 132 CE, the Han dynasty polymath Zhang Heng built the world’s first seismoscope, an instrument using mechanics and gears to discern the cardinal direction of earthquakes up to 500 km away. In 718 CE Gautama Siddha, an astronomer of Indian descent born in Chang’an, translated the Indian Navagraha calendar into Chinese at the throne’s request, bringing with it Indian numerals, the zero, and a table of sines. Eleven years later a Tang meridian survey stretching from northern Vietnam to the steppe produced the Dayan calendar, formulated by the monk-astronomer Yixing.

In 733 CE Gautama Siddha’s son, Gautama Zhuan, formally accused the recently deceased Yixing of plagiarising the Indian work, a charge tied to his own family’s prestige and position. The Tang court did not settle the matter by deciding whose civilisation deserved the credit. It investigated, and found the charge false: the dynastic history records that it sprang from Gautama Zhuan’s resentment at being excluded from the reform, not from any fault in Yixing’s calculations. Historians still debate how much Yixing owed to Indian sources; his use of the tangent almost certainly did. But the court cleared him of copying. The point is that a dispute from 1300 years ago is settled the way historians of science still settle disputes today — by returning to the calculations rather than asking which side one would prefer to be right. It is our argument for engagement between two states that will remain competitors on nearly every other axis. Diplomacy manages disagreement. Law adjudicates it. Science can dissolve it, because a well-posed question about the physical world has an answer that does not care who is asking. Its primary scientific objective, to determine whether the third neutrino mass state is heavier or lighter than the other two, is the same objective JUNO now pursues. In June 2023, radio astronomical pulsar timing arrays around the world announced the first evidence for a background of gravitational waves with periods of years, the probable signature of supermassive black holes spiralling towards each other across the Universe. The Indian Pulsar Timing Array (InPTA) uses the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) near Pune, and they reported findings jointly with their European partners. China’s Pulsar Timing array (CPTA) uses the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) in Guizhou, the largest single radio dish on Earth, and they reported its findings independently.

The two instruments are not duplicates. FAST achieves excellent timing precision on individual millisecond pulsars by virtue of its sheer scale and raw sensitivity. The uGMRT, however, is uniquely capable of observing at much lower radio frequencies (300–500 MHz), where the smearing effect of interstellar plasma, known as the dispersion measure, can be carefully quantified and accounted for. The dynamic nature of the interstellar medium introduces slowly varying time delays in the measured time-of-arrival of pulsar signals, which can mimic or obscure the delays introduced by passing gravitational waves. FAST’s higher-frequency observations cannot easily determine this dispersion measure correction on its own. Put the two datasets together and the measurement gets sharper in a way that neither telescope can achieve alone, just as Zu Chongzhi’s and Aryabhata’s estimates of π were each less useful than the interval they jointly defined. This is not a diplomatic nicety. It is how Nature works: two independent measurements of the same signal reduce the uncertainty on its value in a way neither measurement can on its own. The whole is indeed greater than the sum of its parts. Subterranean synergies: Neutrinos in Jiangmen and Theni A similar dynamic exists in fundamental particle physics. In 2012 the Daya Bay Reactor Neutrino experiment in China, led by physicist Yifang Wang, measured the last unknown mixing angle (θ₁₃) which determines how different flavours of neutrinos transmute through quantum mechanics into each other as they travel through space. Building on this achievement, China’s Institute of High Energy Physics then constructed the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20,000-tonne liquid scintillator detector located 700 m underground and 53 km from the Taishan and Yangjiang nuclear power plants – a distance optimised for maximum sensitivity. JUNO began taking data recently, and involves over 700 scientists from 74 institutions across 17 countries and regions. Noticeably absent from this collaboration is India which for many years has planned its own underground neutrino laboratory, the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO), in the Bodi West Hills of Theni, Tamil Nadu. INO was designed to house a 50,000-tonne magnetised Iron Calorimeter (ICAL) to study atmospheric neutrinos. Its primary scientific objective, to determine whether the third neutrino mass state is heavier or lighter than the other two, is the same objective JUNO now pursues. But the INO project was stalled indefinitely amid baseless environmental litigation and protests instigated by local politicians, leaving a generation of trained Indian particle physicists without a domestic experiment to work on. This is not an argument for political lobbying or for forcing an unnatural partnership. It is simply to emphasise a stark misalignment of resources. Decades of human expertise, built at real financial cost over many years in India, sits geographically adjacent to a Chinese experiment built to use exactly that calibre of expertise. The wall separating the physicists in Theni from the data in Jiangmen is entirely of human construction. It is not a physical barrier, nor is it a boundary recognised by the neutrinos passing harmlessly through the Earth. Its primary scientific objective, to determine whether the third neutrino mass state is heavier or lighter than the other two, is the same objective JUNO now pursues. But the INO project was stalled indefinitely amid baseless environmental litigation and protests instigated by local politicians, leaving a generation of trained Indian particle physicists without a domestic experiment to work on.

This is not an argument for political lobbying or for forcing an unnatural partnership. It is simply to emphasise a stark misalignment of resources. Decades of human expertise, built at real financial cost over many years in India, sits geographically adjacent to a Chinese experiment built to use exactly that calibre of expertise. The wall separating the physicists in Theni from the data in Jiangmen is entirely of human construction. It is not a physical barrier, nor is it a boundary recognised by the neutrinos passing harmlessly through the Earth. The fault lines that bind: Himalayan seismology The Himalaya offers a similar argument in geology. The mountain range forms a single, dynamic tectonic system, regardless of where a political border is drawn through its peaks. On 7th January 2025, a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Tingri County on the southern Tibetan Plateau. The seismic rupture occurred along conjugate normal faults within the Dengmecuo graben, driven by the ongoing east-west extension of the crust. The shockwaves were felt from Kathmandu in Nepal to Patna in northern India. The geopolitical boundary between them means nothing to a propagating seismic wave. The glaciers of this same plateau feed both the Indus and the Brahmaputra river systems; the ecological and hydrological fate of both nations depends on them. Whether they coordinate or not, seismologists in Lhasa and Dehradun are already studying the same fault system from opposite ends. The only variable is whether they do this analysis with each other’s data or without it. In 132 CE, the Han dynasty polymath Zhang Heng built the world’s first seismoscope, an instrument using mechanics and gears to discern the cardinal direction of earthquakes up to 500 km away. His name now graces a newly announced scientific fellowship in Beijing. Were he alive today, the problem of modern data isolation would be immediately apparent to him: a single instrument reveals only that the Earth moved. Understanding why it moved and predicting the next rupture requires more than one vantage point on the same ground. The human element in the age of artificial intelligence Mathematics offers the argument in its purest form, because mathematics needs the least material infrastructure of any science. At the Beijing International Congress of Basic Science last month, the Fields medallist Martin Hairer argued that although artificial intelligence will change how mathematics is done, it will not end it.The Congress Chair Shing-Tung Yau emphasised that while AI will greatly enhance scientific research, the essence of scientific discovery will always depend on human creativity, imagination, and independent thinking. If that diagnosis is right, the scarcest resource of the coming decades will not be computing power but trained human judgement, creativity, and intuition: a resource that neither artificial intelligence nor a single national tradition can manufacture at will. Together, India and China award more first degrees in science and engineering than any other two countries on earth. The Indian National Science Academy (INSA) and the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) ran a formal scientist exchange programme that, over the 24 years between 1995 and 2019, sent a mere 88 Indian scientists to China and brought just 72 Chinese scientists the other way. That is an average of under seven visits a year between the two largest reservoirs of young scientific talent. In the terminology of physics, this is effectively a null result, and such a null result is worth serious analysis. The ascent of a scientific civilisation Over fifty years ago, the Polish-British historian of science Jacob Bronowski concluded his book behind the major BBC television series The Ascent of Man by issuing a stark warning: “If we don’t take the next step in the ascent of man, it will be taken by people elsewhere — in Africa, in China”. He did not name India, a detail that reveals more about the parochialism of England in 1973 than it does about the potential trajectory of the global scientific future. However Bronowski’s underlying test survives the limited vision of his era. He defined the modern world as a scientific civilisation, one in which the integrity of knowledge is the ultimate currency, and argued that the ascent belongs to whoever keeps faith with evidence, not to any specific ethnicity or nation. That test now faces New Delhi and Beijing. It does not require the two governments to trust one another’s geopolitical ambitions. It asks a much smaller, far more answerable question: will their scientists trust each other’s empirical data? The complementary pulsar timing arrays pointed at the nanohertz gravitational wave background, the parallel neutrino physics communities seeking the mass ordering, the shared Himalayan fault lines dictating seismic risk, the vast mathematical talent pools gathering in both capitals: none of these are new diplomatic proposals. They already exist. What is missing is not a sweeping bilateral agreement, a complex visa regime, or a heavily negotiated joint communiqué. What is missing is the much smaller, far less negotiable act of two human beings, standing on either side of a border that neither physics nor mathematics recognises, agreeing to look at the same evidence from Nature and accept what it says. Gautama Zhuan and Yixing’s successors managed to achieve this over a calendar, under an emperor neither of them could disobey. It should not require an emperor for the scientists of India and China to do it again today. editorials.title: From Khirad to Kashaf, Pakistani dramas are rewriting what it means to be a ‘good’ woman

And when Khirad Ahsan cried, silently, alone in a room, the women in my house would watch her, not out of sadness, but recognition. Her one act of rebellion is leaving. When the truth finally surfaces and Ashar comes back begging forgiveness, she gives it.

She is falsely accused of infidelity and is manipulated out of her own daughter’s custody by a jealous mother-in-law. Khirad spends most of the drama absorbing all of it.

Her one act of rebellion is leaving. When the truth finally surfaces and Ashar comes back begging forgiveness, she gives it.

That ending mattered because Humsafar was, at its heart, a love story. The question was not simply whether a wronged woman could rebuild her life, but whether romance and marriage can eventually be restored. For the women in my house, that was a familiar language. They had grown up with the idea that sabr (patience) was one of the highest virtues a woman could have. Don’t answer every insult. Endure with dignity. Let time reveal who was right. Khirad wasn’t alone. Around the same time, many similar characters came into being. Sara in Meri Zaat Zarra e Benishan (2009) is arguably the prototype — a woman betrayed by nearly everyone she loves, she is accused of infidelity, suffers an abusive marriage, and processes her pain only through devotion rather than defiance. Her suffering is filmed almost like martyrdom. Mazloom , but never bitter. Wronged, but never vengeful. These characters represented the idea of a “good” woman for the women in my house. They watched them and felt seen. Because there was comfort in a female lead who suffered exactly the way you’d been told suffering was supposed to look like. A pragmatic woman Then came Kashaf Murtaza. Zindagi Gulzar Hai (2012) is remembered as one of the most beloved Pakistani dramas ever made, the one that turned Fawad Khan and Sanam Saeed into household names. But when it first aired, Kashaf did not land the way Khirad had. She wasn’t soft or patient in the sanctioned way. She was the eldest daughter of a lower-middle-class family, abandoned by a father who’d taken a second wife. She’d hardened into someone pragmatic and guarded, and this was the part that unsettled people. This was also the drama where the plot began leaning away from pure romance. Kashaf’s arc was really about class, education, and self-respect. The women in my house didn’t immediately warm up to her. “ She doesn’t trust anyone .” “ Why is she so angry all the time? It’s off-putting .” For them, Kashaf lacked the tehzeeb , the grace, that made a struggling female lead sympathetic. But something happened over the years of reruns that followed. Zindagi TV in India alone aired it multiple times. The very people in my house who’d found her difficult started to see that Kashaf’s hardness wasn’t a flaw. Her ambition to finish her education, get a government job, and build a life that didn’t depend on any man’s mercy was framed as the moral centre of the show, not a character defect she needed to be cured of. By the time she stood on her own feet, choosing Zaroon rather than just needing him, the same women who’d once called her “hard” had started calling her “practical”. The discomfort didn’t vanish overnight. Khirad was still the favorite, but the shift towards Kashaf did not go unnoticed. Also read: Malayalam cinema never had it so good. Big box office hits, OTT global reach Who is a ‘strong woman’? By the late-2010s, something had shifted in what a “strong woman” drama was even trying to do. Yaqeen Ka Safar (2017) gave us Zubia, played by Sajal Aly. She plays a woman whose mother is killed by her abusive father, who is then manipulated and nearly assaulted by a man she trusted, and who is thrown out of her own home by her brother and sister-in-law for the “shame” of what was done to her. But the drama’s real innovation was refusing to let that be the end of her story. Zubia rebuilds herself, alone, into a doctor. She re-enters the narrative as someone with a career, autonomy, and eventually a love story she gets to choose on her own terms, well after she rebuilds herself. This is the phase where I think the shift in my house really took hold. Because the drama still portrayed sympathy for the suffering, but the suffering was no longer the moral of the story. Then came Cheekh’s (2019), Mannat, played by Saba Qamar, which saw a female lead do something Khirad never would have: fight publicly, loudly, and at enormous personal cost, for someone else’s justice rather than her own comfort. It played out as a crime thriller, almost entirely uninterested in romance as a driving force. The drama’s most quoted scene has her standing in a courtroom, fighting her friend’s case against the antagonist, refusing to let his power write the ending. This was the first time I saw the women in my house watching a crime thriller Pakistani drama, not questioning the absence of romance or silent sabr but actually invested in the story and rooting for Mannat and her fight for justice. A new female lead Which brings us to now, and to a set of unapologetically unconventional women. Most of these dramas, interestingly, are now built as social dramas, thrillers, character studies, rather than mere romance. The latest example is Beena, played by Urwa Hocane in Aapki Izzat . Beena has a 14-year marriage with Tabish, who becomes increasingly cruel as his social and political ambitions grow. He humiliates her, wants a second marriage, and invokes religion to justify that decision. Normally, the conventional female lead would have endured it all. But 2026 Beena? With no other weapons to fight, she runs away, taking a fair share of Tabish’s money, with another man, not because she loved or needed him, but because she felt this was the only way to humiliate Tabish. When Tabish invokes his “religious right” to remarry, Beena unflinchingly questions the selective way he is using religion, asking whether faith is a principle he genuinely lives by or a shield he uses conveniently, shaming him to the point that he cries. My mother was hooting at this point. There’s no romance left to protect here. The marriage itself is the thing being examined. Watching these dramas, there was no great ideological awakening in our drawing room. Nobody watched Zindagi Gulzar Hai and woke up the next morning with a new understanding of feminism. There were just years of television, reruns, and conversations. One woman after another entered the screen and slowly widened the definition of strength and empowerment. She plays a woman whose mother is killed by her abusive father, who is then manipulated and nearly assaulted by a man she trusted, and who is thrown out of her own home by her brother and sister-in-law for the “shame” of what was done to her. But the drama’s real innovation was refusing to let that be the end of her story. Zubia rebuilds herself, alone, into a doctor. She re-enters the narrative as someone with a career, autonomy, and eventually a love story she gets to choose on her own terms, well after she rebuilds herself. This is the phase where I think the shift in my house really took hold. Because the drama still portrayed sympathy for the suffering, but the suffering was no longer the moral of the story. Then came Cheekh’s (2019), Mannat, played by Saba Qamar, which saw a female lead do something Khirad never would have: fight publicly, loudly, and at enormous personal cost, for someone else’s justice rather than her own comfort. It played out as a crime thriller, almost entirely uninterested in romance as a driving force. The drama’s most quoted scene has her standing in a courtroom, fighting her friend’s case against the antagonist, refusing to let his power write the ending. This was the first time I saw the women in my house watching a crime thriller Pakistani drama, not questioning the absence of romance or silent sabr but actually invested in the story and rooting for Mannat and her fight for justice. A new female lead Which brings us to now, and to a set of unapologetically unconventional women. Most of these dramas, interestingly, are now built as social dramas, thrillers, character studies, rather than mere romance. The latest example is Beena, played by Urwa Hocane in Aapki Izzat . Beena has a 14-year marriage with Tabish, who becomes increasingly cruel as his social and political ambitions grow. He humiliates her, wants a second marriage, and invokes religion to justify that decision. Normally, the conventional female lead would have endured it all. But 2026 Beena? With no other weapons to fight, she runs away, taking a fair share of Tabish’s money, with another man, not because she loved or needed him, but because she felt this was the only way to humiliate Tabish. When Tabish invokes his “religious right” to remarry, Beena unflinchingly questions the selective way he is using religion, asking whether faith is a principle he genuinely lives by or a shield he uses conveniently, shaming him to the point that he cries. My mother was hooting at this point. There’s no romance left to protect here. The marriage itself is the thing being examined. Watching these dramas, there was no great ideological awakening in our drawing room. Nobody watched Zindagi Gulzar Hai and woke up the next morning with a new understanding of feminism. There were just years of television, reruns, and conversations. One woman after another entered the screen and slowly widened the definition of strength and empowerment. I know it worked because my mother and khala no longer have patience for characters who spend entire episodes forgiving and quietly accepting what is being done to her; one of them will eventually say, “Yaar, kuch toh karo.” (Edited by Janaki Pande)

Mazloom , but never bitter. Wronged, but never vengeful. These characters represented the idea of a “good” woman for the women in my house. They watched them and felt seen. Because there was comfort in a female lead who suffered exactly the way you’d been told suffering was supposed to look like.

Zindagi Gulzar Hai (2012) is remembered as one of the most beloved Pakistani dramas ever made, the one that turned Fawad Khan and Sanam Saeed into household names. She was the eldest daughter of a lower-middle-class family, abandoned by a father who’d taken a second wife. She’d hardened into someone pragmatic and guarded, and this was the part that unsettled people. This was also the drama where the plot began leaning away from pure romance. Kashaf’s arc was really about class, education, and self-respect. The women in my house didn’t immediately warm up to her. “ She doesn’t trust anyone .” “ Why is she so angry all the time? It’s off-putting .” For them, Kashaf lacked the tehzeeb , the grace, that made a struggling female lead sympathetic. But something happened over the years of reruns that followed. Zindagi TV in India alone aired it multiple times. The very people in my house who’d found her difficult started to see that Kashaf’s hardness wasn’t a flaw. Her ambition to finish her education, get a government job, and build a life that didn’t depend on any man’s mercy was framed as the moral centre of the show, not a character defect she needed to be cured of. By the time she stood on her own feet, choosing Zaroon rather than just needing him, the same women who’d once called her “hard” had started calling her “practical”. With no other weapons to fight, she runs away, taking a fair share of Tabish’s money, with another man, not because she loved or needed him, but because she felt this was the only way to humiliate Tabish. When Tabish invokes his “religious right” to remarry, Beena unflinchingly questions the selective way he is using religion, asking whether faith is a principle he genuinely lives by or a shield he uses conveniently, shaming him to the point that he cries. My mother was hooting at this point. There’s no romance left to protect here. The marriage itself is the thing being examined. Watching these dramas, there was no great ideological awakening in our drawing room. Nobody watched Zindagi Gulzar Hai and woke up the next morning with a new understanding of feminism. There were just years of television, reruns, and conversations. One woman after another entered the screen and slowly widened the definition of strength and empowerment. I know it worked because my mother and khala no longer have patience for characters who spend entire episodes forgiving and quietly accepting what is being done to her; one of them will eventually say, “Yaar, kuch toh karo.” (Edited by Janaki Pande)

editorials.title: Xi-Modi BRICS meeting signals thaw in ties. The Chinese say it is at a fragile stage
editorials.passage:
C hinese President Xi Jinping visited India after seven years, marking his first bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Indian soil since Mamallapuram in 2019. The Xi-Modi bilateral talk lasted about 45 minutes and covered the standard issues of the border, trade, and regional and global affairs. Xi’s presence in New Delhi became a hotly discussed topic across Chinese internet platforms, with much of the discussion suggesting that China and India are warming up to each other. Warming of ties? A commentary on Baijiahao noted that even with conflict and competition, communication never stopped between the two countries. This, it said, is the clearest signal from the China-India meeting and the basis for maintaining stable relations between the two major Asian powers. Xie Chao , associate research fellow at Fudan University’s Center for South Asian Studies, pointed out that the easing of tensions is evident in the last two years. Following Modi’s re-election in 2024, he said, India began showing signs of substantially fixing ties with China, alongside greater introspection on the costs of its confrontational policies toward Beijing.

Following Modi’s re-election in 2024, he said, India began showing signs of substantially fixing ties with China, alongside greater introspection on the costs of its confrontational policies toward Beijing.

Much of the Chinese coverage has focused on cooperation in multilateral settings. Zhang Shuai, deputy director of the Center for Indian Studies at Lanzhou University and associate professor at the Belt and Road Research Center, contends that China and India see multilateral cooperation as an important tool for stabilising bilateral relations. Similarly, Victor Gao, Chair Professor at Soochow University and deputy director of the Center for China and Globalization, views the BRICS summit as an opportunity for China and India to exchange views, reach greater consensus on international issues and even discuss the territorial dispute. But the Chinese views are also skeptical about how far the improvement in ties can go. A new normal and its limits Hu Shisheng , deputy secretary-general of the Academic Committee of the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, described China-India ties as entering a new normal. It is stabilising after a decline, slowly recovering, and coexisting with competition. For Hu, this is a bottoming-out process, and cannot be called a reset. India’s shift, he argued, has been driven largely by real-world pressures, while the US factor is both pushing the two sides toward each other and limiting their relationship too. This cautious assessment runs through other Chinese commentary. Lin Minwang, researcher and deputy dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University, sees the relationship as improving but fragile. He pointed to the scope for economic cooperation, particularly as India seeks greater Chinese investment, while criticising restrictions on Chinese companies and visas. For Lin, reciprocity and mutual benefit will be important tests of whether India is genuinely prepared to move closer to China or is simply seeking greater room for manoeuvre while remaining dependent on the US. Zhang Sinan, a media commentator, similarly argue d that India is unlikely to abandon its traditional position but will seek greater strategic space. The limits are particularly clear on security. Another comment noted that the border remains unresolved and strategic trust is far from restored. India’s cooperation with China in BRICS alongside its continued participation in the US-led Quad is interpreted as part of a hedging strategy. The implication is that the thaw will remain uneven. Economic interests nevertheless provide a reason to keep the relationship moving. A report by the Shanghai-based The Paper described the “ melting of ice and snow” as a process that cannot happen overnight. From Kazan to New Delhi, it argued, progress will depend on both sides meeting each other halfway, maintaining candid communication and pursuing pragmatic cooperation. Li Hongmei, researcher at the South Asia Research Center of the Shanghai Institute for International Studies, points to international instability, India’s uncertainty over the US and shared development needs as drivers of cooperation. Economic interdependence also matters, with China becoming India’s largest trading partner in 2025-26. But Li sees the détente as pragmatic rather than strategic. India is gradually easing visa and investment restrictions while maintaining security concerns over China’s role in South Asia. Border tensions, China-Pakistan relations, the Dalai Lama issue, trade imbalances and China’s growing presence in South Asia continue to complicate the relationship. The same contradiction is evident in economic ties. One commentator argued that Modi’s ‘Make in India’ ambitions remain heavily dependent on Chinese supply chains even as New Delhi continues efforts to counter China politically and strategically. Damaged political trust, the border dispute and efforts to diversify away from China limit the scope for deeper economic cooperation. Stable border, a predictable business environment and greater mutual trust, the commentator argued, will be necessary if economic ties are to expand. Interestingly, there is less hardline commentary calling for confrontation than before. One commentator sees t he border tensions as part of a wider competition driven by India’s military build-up, nationalism, economic restrictions on China and closer alignment with the US. Yet the argument is that China should avoid both war and retreat. The preferred approach, according to the Chinese commentary, should be firm but restrained where it has to maintain border positions and deterrence, respond proportionately, keep negotiations going and avoid a prolonged confrontation. The border dispute, in this view, is more likely to require sustained management than a one-off settlement. Also read: The real BRICS story is what China, Russia want & India wishes A fragile thaw This time around, the discussion on the Chinese internet is more cautious than openly hostile or provocative. Much of it is critical of India’s handling of the border issue, but it also sees India-China ties moving toward normalcy. At the same time, there is caution about the durability of the thaw. At best, it remains fragile, with the underlying differences continuing to influence India’s China policy. The border remains the biggest irritant and a major source of strategic mistrust. Commercial differences persist too, while India’s pursuit of strategic autonomy, including closer cooperation with the West, remains an important part of its foreign policy. The setting of Xi’s visit is also telling. The Modi-Xi meeting took place on the sidelines of BRICS. Xi did not make a special trip to India focused on the bilateral relationship or addressing its underlying problems. Clearly, the relationship has not returned to the pre-2020 status quo, and there is little indication that it will do so soon. Hu Shisheng described this as a “new normal”. This perhaps best sums up where India-China ties stand after Xi’s New Delhi visit. But the future direction of India-China ties will depend on multiple factors. One high-level meeting can provide support and momentum, but it will take much more than that. It will also require a change in the narrative and a better understanding of India’s concerns and agency. Otherwise, the thaw and stability will remain fragile and temporary. Sana Hashmi, PhD, is a fellow at the Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation. She tweets @sanahashmi1. Views are personal. (Edited by Ratan Priya)

editorials.title: India wants more cars, buses, 2-wheelers. Manufacturers are struggling to catch up
editorials.passage:
“W e don’t like to experiment on customers”. This is what Maruti Suzuki’s Partho Banerjee told me at the launch of the face-lifted Baleno. Thousands of production Balenos are parked at the manufacturer’s yards and will soon be delivered once the final certification is done. “My sales head and dealers are screaming for more cars, but I don’t want to send products until all clearances are done,” said Banerjee, Senior Executive Officer (Marketing & Sales) at Maruti Suzuki India. This was in context of the fact that Maruti Suzuki has a huge waiting period for vehicles as it heads into the festive season. While Banerjee didn’t give estimates, the manufacturer’s pending bookings are believed to have reached around 1.8 lakh . That is half the annual production of a single average automotive production line. “Take the Brezza, we have over 60,000 bookings but production and sales are only around 15,000 units every month,” he said, mentioning that while the demand might seem great, dealers are having to turn away customers. “A problem of plenty is a problem after all. I don’t want to lose customers.”

While Banerjee didn’t give estimates, the manufacturer’s pending bookings are believed to have reached around 1.8 lakh . That is half the annual production of a single average automotive production line. “Take the Brezza, we have over 60,000 bookings but production and sales are only around 15,000 units every month,” he said, mentioning that while the demand might seem great, dealers are having to turn away customers. “A problem of plenty is a problem after all. I don’t want to lose customers.”

This was in context of the fact that Maruti Suzuki has a huge waiting period for vehicles as it heads into the festive season. While Banerjee didn’t give estimates, the manufacturer’s pending bookings are believed to have reached around 1.8 lakh . That is half the annual production of a single average automotive production line.

“Take the Brezza, we have over 60,000 bookings but production and sales are only around 15,000 units every month,” he said, mentioning that while the demand might seem great, dealers are having to turn away customers. “A problem of plenty is a problem after all. I don’t want to lose customers.”

He need not worry, the Indian automotive market is on a tear unlike any other. The post-Covid sales jump shows no sign of slowing down. The passenger vehicle sales in August were a shade under 4.5 lakh units. But Banerjee believes that number could touch over 5.5 lakh units if Maruti Suzuki and certain other manufacturers enhance their capacity. “Things should ease up for us by early 2027,” he said, pointing to the fact that the company’s Hansalpur plant in Gujarat touched an installed capacity of over a million, the first single site in India to achieve this feat . Will the growth sustain? It is not just Maruti Suzuki that is facing a problem of plenty. Kia India Managing Director and CEO Gwanggu Lee told me at the launch of the new Sorento that while Kia had enough capacity for now, with monthly sales crossing 30,000 units, the Korean carmaker was starting the process of adding capacity within the next few years. Can such outstanding growth, over ten per cent year-on-year in August, carry on? Shailesh Chandra, MD and CEO of Tata Motors, which was the fastest growing carmaker in August with year-on-year growth in domestic passenger vehicle dispatches climbing an exceptional 59 per cent, did point out that the ‘base effect’ will kick in soon. “Car sales really began to shoot upwards after the GST 2.0 norms kicked in around October last year. So growth numbers will start moderating because of the base effect,” Chandra said at the annual conference of the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM). “But full-year sales will be way in excess of five million”. Also read: New Volvo EX90 feels and looks Chinese. That’s what makes it so good The capacity problem And it isn’t just passenger vehicles that are booming, the big opportunity, as Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari mentioned at the SIAM conference, is in buses. Anyone who drives through the Indian urban morass knows that public transit buses are few and far between. India has less than two buses per thousand people and needs closer to eight. And not petrol and diesel buses, but electric ones, according to the minister. But again, capacity is a problem. The country needs to produce 1,50,000 electric buses per annum but can currently make just 70,000. While Gadkari urged manufacturers to ramp up production , new manufacturers like Pune-based EKA Mobility are stepping up to the task. Sudhir Mehta, Founder and Chairman of the EV manufacturer , told me that the company will soon be introducing 18-metre articulated electric buses in India. “There are requirements for all sorts of electric buses over the next few years, from nine-metre last-mile connectors to these articulated buses. And also long-distance buses. But the challenges will not be around building these buses but charging them, and that is where battery and charging innovation will come,” said Mehta. Two-wheelers and tractors are booming as well, and that does address many of the concerns around GDP growth. This is because, according to SIAM, 47 per cent of India’s manufacturing GDP comes from the automotive industry. Now capacity is being added, and with India having a penetration of just 24 cars per thousand population, even getting to 50 cars per thousand will mean continued growth for the next decade. But as you might have seen in my video tour of Mahindra’s EV plant at Chakan near Pune , the massive increase in demand for cars, buses, and two-wheelers isn’t leading to a commensurate increase in jobs. Most automotive factories today are examples of extreme automation — with welding robots to little cat-like robots hauling equipment around. Incidentally, automation isn’t about saving money anymore, it’s also about safety, especially in construction. Kushan Mitra is an automotive journalist based in New Delhi. He tweets @kushanmitra. Views are personal. (Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

editorials.title: Durga Puja doesn’t need DJs. Banning them isn’t anti-Bengali
editorials.passage:
W hen the BJP swept the West Bengal A ssembly elections in May, it evidently ruffled feathers among a few Bengalis, especially the self-proclaimed ‘ bhadroloks ’. They suspected that a change at the helm meant a shift in the Bengali way of life . And to no one’s surprise, Durga Puja, in the very first year of the BJP’s reign, has found itself at the centre of a heated cultural, religious, and political debate. Among a series of new rules for Durga Puja, the Suvendu Adhikar i -led government decided to ban DJs in pandals and immersion processions. Like other changes, this too triggered a widespread controversy, with critics and opposition parties strongly opposing the move, saying it is an attempt ‘to alter West Bengal’s cultural and religious identity’. To begin with, DJs were never a part of Bengali culture or tradition. It emerged during the TMC’s 15-year rule. The high-decibel DJ music played during immersion processions is a modern addition that disrupts the traditional sanctity of Durga Puja, replacing heritage elements like the ‘dhak’ (traditional Bengali drums) and ‘shonkho’ (conch shells).
