editorials.title: ‘It is past and contemporary. And alive’: Writer Janice Pariat’s summer of living among archives
editorials.passage:
There are three things to know about archives.

We are blissfully unaware of all this as we make our way to the first of our library stops this summer. The British Library. Big, Brutalist, red-bricked, stone-paved, and in one corner, perpetually in attendance, Paolozzi’s naked Newton hunched over a pair of dividers. I’ve been here a few times before, my husband, Sam hasn’t, and inside we take a moment to gaze at that very high ceiling, white, light-filled, and before us, the gigantic bookshelves, end to end – we still wonder whether they’re merely decorative. It doesn’t take long for both of us to be handed our reader’s passes downstairs, and we’re thrilled.

Then we spend an eternity at the locker room.

Narrow corridors lined with lockers, most of which are full, faulty or stubbornly stuck. After we eventually find one that works, and take a picture of the locker number, we head upstairs with our see-through bags holding essentials. No water. No pens. No jackets. Just laptop, phone, wallet, notebook.

Given the nature of our interests, we’re directed to The Asian and African Studies Reading Room (AAS RR). Third floor and consistently busy. Later in the month, I happen to venture into Rare Books and Maps, and marvel at how quiet they are compared to the AAS RR.

It’s a large space, high-ceilinged, walls lined with portraits – Indian princes? I register vaguely – and bookshelves. We are guided, by a friendly librarian, on how to use the catalogue, log in, search, request, and off we go.

Except, of course, we realise, that the catalogue is its own beast.

And that like the archives it gives up its secrets slowly.

My first search turns up zero results.

My second is a little more yielding.

Somehow, we manage to request books for the next day. We decide we’ve done enough for Day One and walk ourselves across to Bloomsbury to a favourite café – St John’s at the London Review bookshop. We drink tea, eat madeleines, admire our reader passes. All the while, I brace myself for a full and busy month.

And it is. Almost every day in the reading room. Requesting the right books, and often the wrong ones. Failure says the email. This shelf mark does not exist. Your details don’t match. Turns out, I’m repeatedly entering incorrect information into the request form. I try again, and again. Half an hour later, if I’m lucky, Your request is waiting to be picked up.

It is slow, deliberate, and wonderfully patience-inducing.

I learn key words. Old British spellings for Khasi: Cossyah, Cassia, among others. And then the records are brought out by the world’s loveliest librarians. One by one, huge, heavy, each in their own grey cardboard box tied with string. The India Office record books themselves are a stain-y, rusty red, and I learn not to wear white on archive days.

I carry three folders at a time to my table. Strength training, I tell myself. But honestly that’s not the hardest part. Perhaps we forget that libraries, archives, reading rooms are decidedly demanding spaces on the body. The endless sitting, peering, squinting. The long posture of seeking. The careful holding, opening, unfolding, of a historical volume. And when one is permitted, the awkward positioning of arm and hand to take photographs. A few hours in, and I ache – my back, my shoulders, my neck. I stand, I walk, I step outside to drink some water. But there’s no time to waste, there’s so much to get through, and soon I’m back in my seat again.

I notice the dust early on. It leaves a residue on my fingers as I turn the pages. It makes me sneeze. It catches in my throat. It thinly films the table long after I’ve returned the items. It gets on my clothes. It has a distinct indescribable smell. Of oldness, and delight, of many summers, and winters, of cupboards, of many, many hands. It reminds me of what Carolyn Steedman says in her book on archives, titled… Dust –

It’s the dust of the workers who made the papers and parchments; the dust of the animals who provided the skins for their leather bindings. I inhale, as she calls it, the “by-product of all the filthy trades that have, by circuitous routes, deposited their end-products in the archives”.

It’s a thrilling prospect.

The archive is alive before me, and in me too.

Steedman offers an extraordinary observation about Derrida's original lecture on Archive Fever : it took place inside Freud’s former home, which was simultaneously a house, museum and archive.

She calls this “an archive in process, taking place at that moment.”

Archives can make us imagine that history is somehow over there . In the folders. In the past.

But the moment we sit down, read the papers, something shifts now . My presence is now.

As are my questions, my interpretations. Political meaning is now. The landscape in which those documents were produced is now. And the archive itself is still doing something now .

An archive is past and contemporary.

Moving through my hands, my fingers, my lungs.

There must be a word for it: this growing addiction to archives.

Every morning, the thrill of heading into the almost unknown.

Who knows what a dusty folder might today reveal?

Nothing and everything. A missing piece of the puzzle. A new trail.

In the archive, one wishes to go on and on. Down another road, round another corner.

Mostly because it holds infinite potential to surprise.

A letter, for instance, from the Workers’ Union in Golder’s Green, London, written on May 9, 1927, in solidarity with workers in Lucknow, “alleged to have conspired to overthrow the present government” and sentenced to death, transportation for life, and years of rigorous imprisonment.

My branch protests against such savage and vindictive sentences on Workers “rightly struggling to be free.”

A finding that has little to do with my research but much to do with heart.

Ann Laura Stoler, in Along the Archival Grain , describes this as when “the archive pulses erratically with affective and political excess.”

I say that at moments like these you can hear it.

Sometimes the archive sings.

The dust reminds me too of all things material and immaterial.

It is proof that something exists, existed, and that it also doesn’t.

So much in the archive, and so much that isn’t.

“Dust, you see, Steedman reminds us, “Will always do this: be both there and not there; what is left and what is gone.”

Within a letter, a reference to a map, which is missing.

Another time, I receive an email saying my requested item is too fragile to be delivered to the reading room. A map of Dibrugarh, Assam, in the 1920s. Somewhere it is slowly turning to dust.

Then a note about a person I simply cannot trace. The archive is bumpy and uneven. At times, thoroughly wild and disorderly. To read along the archival grain, Stoler reminds us, draws our sensibilities to the archive’s granular rather than seamless texture.

How much of an archive is lost, how much cleaned up.

I long to hear the voices of the Khasi chiefs going to war. Of the Khasi “raiders” who swept into Sylhet when their markets were closed to them as a punitive measure. Of the Maram chiefs whose resistance against the British was long and enduring. Of the Jaintia king, swiftly, suddenly, deposed of his throne.

An archive is such a one-sided thing.

But it’s true, what Steedman says, that “silences and absences…always speak to us.

They are their own story. We read what’s there as much as what’s not there.

I left the British Library at the end of June. Dusty. Joyful. Because I had gathered so much. Anxious. Because there was still so much left to gather.

It’s a lesson I learn slowly. Grudgingly.

That there is, as Steedman says, the great, brown, slow-moving strandless river of Everything, and then there is its tiny flotsam that has ended up in the record office you are at work in – and from that, the bits you’ve gathered that amount to not much more than dust.

The archive is endless. Incomplete. But endless.

And at some point, we must let it go.

After London, I learn the archive is moody.

Capable of immense generosity – as well as brutally slamming the door in your face.

I receive an email from the librarian at Nottingham University, deeply apologetic, saying that the archive there, the one I’d have liked to see, is closed for the entire summer. They are moving buildings.

And all at once it felt like trails had been cut off. Stories missed. Voices silenced.

Don’t be dramatic, I told myself. This has closed, so something else may be found.

Though this thought only after I first wept and wept with annoyance.

At Edinburgh’s National Library of Scotland, we must offer up our see-through bags for inspection, along with our pencil cases, before entering a reading room with windows all along one side that overlook the city, and in the distance, Arthur’s Seat. It is distracting. But I still try and catch a window spot if I can.

Here, I’m helped by a group of friendly, ever-efficient librarians. One guides me to the National Records of Scotland for a collection of letters the NLS don’t hold, and another prepares the Crawford Papers for me in meticulous order. The Crawford Papers are on loan from the Crawford and Balcarres family – descendants of Robert Lindsay, collector of Sylhet between 1778 and 1790. He was privy to dramatic scenes involving “Cossyah” raiding parties, and he also traded, hugely, in limestone from the Khasi Hills. It turns out I’d committed a grave error by not notifying the library in advance of my wish to access the papers – Lord Crawford’s assent must be procured, and a massive hunt ensues for the Lord’s email address. Thankfully, it is found. His permission granted. And for days after, I sit in my corner, hurled back to the late 1700s through letters, account books, memoranda, and notes. It is fortunate, it turns out, that my Nottingham days are spent in Edinburgh instead. The papers are extensive. I would’ve struggled to rush through them, especially because photographs are not permitted and I must make copious notes by hand. At this, I am mostly terrible. Panick stricken by what I might miss. Also, how strange to copy someone else’s words, someone else’s hands. It is admittedly tedious too. By the end of the day, I emerge blinking and bug-eyed.

Perhaps this is why it is only when we step outside one Sunday, take a train, and then a bus to Colinsburgh, where the Crawford’s Balcarres Estate is located, that the archive suddenly feels tangible and alive.

Walking through the gardens, standing beside the 200-year-old yew hedges, gazing at the purple campanula. It is raining. It’s cold. The grass is springy. The house is shrouded in fog. We are looking at the world in which those pages in the library, those scraps of paper, were produced – and which, in turn, helped produce the estate too.

Archive, I am reminded, is land, tree, hedge, gate. It is brick and stone. It is garden.

It is landscape that outlives all who wrote those pages.

In Wales, the National Library overlooks the sea.

It is on a hill, and below it lies Aberystwyth, a little coastal town, and then the deep, endless blue of the Atlantic. Is it my favourite library? Yes. For these reasons and more. The café is wonderful, and reasonably priced. The staff friendliest. And there are gardens in bloom all around the building. Perfect for a spot of breakfast or a mid-day coffee break on a bench.

Oddly enough, this is where I find the most material directly linked to the Khasi Hills.

Though this ought not to be surprising, considering the Welsh Missionaries were pottering about there since the 1840s, desperately trying to convert the hill people, and for decades, failing. Many letters then, about rain and loneliness, and later, from the early 1900s onwards, many photographs of serious-faced missionaries. Many maps too. One so large it takes three of us to unroll it onto the special raised maps table. “I might need a drone,” I tell the two librarians who helped me, and since there is ne’re one in sight, they kindly bring me a stool on which I can stand to take photographs. They’re young, funny, friendly, cool – and I find myself imagining that if ever we were to move to Aberystwyth, I’d really like to be friends with them.

The archive days here are quiet – the reading room feels more spacious, less bustle-y than at the BL or Edinburgh. On some mornings, if I get in early enough, I’m the only reader there.

It helps also, I think, that I’ve developed a little system of collecting material. Always take a photo of the request slip before you begin documenting the material. Always note the shelf mark. At the BL, at the beginning, it was all a bit hasty and disorderly. By the end of July, I’m the archive queen.

But despite the neatness, with each item requested, photographed, filed away, I’m reminded by Steedman that here all is media res, that you find nothing in the archive but stories caught halfway through: the middle of things; discontinuities.” “Nothing starts in the Archive,” she says, and I’d add, nothing ends here either.

Except your days at the reading room.

All time at the archives is limited. There will always be a penultimate day, a last day. Then “trains to catch, or flights. Journeys planned. A life elsewhere.” But I spend my last day there – to my astonishment – in great calm. Gone is archive FOMO. I’ve done my best. I let it go. At each library, I’ve thanked the librarians. For one, at Edinburgh, who helped me access the Crawford Papers, I gift a box of matcha cookies. My only sadness is that on my last day at the library in Aberystwyth, my I-wish-I-could-be-friends-with-them librarians aren’t there. So, I say goodbye to the ones I met just that morning. Who’ve also shown me, like all the others, much kindness. And patience. And care to bring out items in the order that you wish to read them. It has been a joy.

In their own time, for two months, each archive was home.

editorials.title: The voice in the din: Why Vidyanand Bapat is making noise about noise
editorials.passage:
On September 3, as Pune resident Vidyanand Bapat was being interviewed by a TV journalist on the busy Tilak Road, a man stepped up and slapped him.

Bapat had been talking about the problem of noise pollution during the Ganesh festival – the city’s most enthusiastic public celebration. Even as the cameraperson and others tried to pull the attacker away, he broke free and tried to hit 37-year-old Bapat again, abusing him for “ speaking against Hindu festivals ”.

Days earlier, on August 24, Bapat – a resident of Narayan Peth in the old city area – had expressed the same concerns at a public meeting called by the municipal corporation on preparations for the Ganesh festival. Members of some of Pune’s hundreds of Ganesh mandals were also present.

Bapat told Scroll about his concerns. “Festival enthusiasts should ensure their celebrations should not become a punishment for citizens who just happen to reside in the vicinity,” he said.

His remarks about high-volume sound systems and the dhol tasha – a traditional part of the celebrations, involving large groups playing huge drums – sparked such an outcry that the police had to escort him out of the premises.

Bapat told Scroll that the furore was not unexpected. “Festival enthusiasts don’t have any logical arguments,” he said.

Even as his crusade against noise pollution has only gathered steam since then, it has angered others. Edited excerpts from an interview:

Some say Indian cities are noisy and heavily populated and that is just the way of life with festivals being one part of it.

Noise should be bifurcated into two types. One is avoidable and the second one is unavoidable. The first type of noise is, for example, from power generators or pneumatic drills or railway engines. It’s because of their high-scale of operation but they are not meant for sound amplification.

The second type of noise is being generated deliberately with the only intention of generating noise – such as using loudspeakers, which is a piece of equipment whose sole purpose is to amplify sound, or performing on musical instruments such as drums and tom toms.

Regarding the first one, there are noise mitigation measures – like today’s power generators have a silent feature. But regarding the second one, their very purpose is sound amplification.

To get rid of this second type of noise pollution, the only recourse is to keep it limited to those who enjoy it. This could be achieved by playing it inside an enclosed or sound-proofed environment. They also need not have to worry about the decibel level because they can play those loud speakers or musical instruments at whatever decibel level they are comfortable with. So this is a win-win solution.

Dhol tasha [drum] groups say many people enjoy watching the performance and that only few others are inconvenienced. And that it’s not possible to celebrate a public festival inside an auditorium.

Some people might be enjoying dhol tasha, but that cannot become a punishment for others. Sawai Gandharva is a classical music festival. But for several years, it has been held in an open ground under a tent.

So what’s the problem with dhol tasha drums and tom toms? They can also easily be played inside an enclosed and soundproof auditorium. And if it is not possible to build an auditorium of sufficient capacity, then you can build a new one with your own contribution and broadcast that performance – like a cricket match.

Your enjoyment should not be a punishment for a few others.

Ganesh mandals and dhol tasha groups feel that the noise only affects a few people.

The majority-minority logic is again ridiculous. It’s logically fallacious. It’s called the bandwagon fallacy or ad populism fallacy, which basically means that something is right just because a majority of people are saying, at this moment, that it is right.

In the time of Galileo and [Giordano] Bruno, almost 99% of the people were saying that Earth is flat, and the sun revolves around the Earth because that’s what was visible to the naked eye. When Galileo put forth his discovery that Earth was round and revolves around the sun, it was opposed by the Catholic Church and everyone.

So just because something is popular in a period doesn’t mean that it is objectively correct. Many people are getting disturbed by this noise pollution under the pretext of festival celebration. So, the festival enthusiasts should address that concern and they should not resort to this ad populism fallacy that those who are in the minority should tolerate whatever we do.

You have set off an important debate. Have you got a lot of support and how do you see it going forward?

Since the last two weeks, I have been contacted by many citizens throughout Maharashtra and even the rest of India. Many citizens have contacted me and said they are supporting the cause that I am fighting for.

Citizen activism has increased a lot around noise pollution and traffic obstruction under the pretext of public festival celebrations. That is the part and parcel of any functioning democracy.

Otherwise, although the elections are being held, so-called democracy gets converted into electoral despotism. Elected representatives start acting like autocrats. To prevent a constitutional democracy from operating as an autocracy, or electoral despotism, citizen activism is a necessity.

It looks like the cause that I was fighting for, at my personal level, in the near future it will take the shape of an organised movement.

I don’t know if you are allowed to talk about a lawyer sending you a legal notice demanding an apology for insulting Hindu gods. Some also say as you have openly identified as an atheist and have no right to speak about religion.

That so-called notice is a joke. That is not a legal notice. We can shred it and throw it in the dustbin. I haven’t received it through official means – through a registered post.

Regarding being an atheist, believing in any religion or not believing in any religion is entirely a personal matter. That doesn’t deprive you of your right to speak about issues that are faced at a societal level.

Despite categorically saying that I am opposing only noise pollution and traffic obstructions, not the festival in its entirety, still they are trying to pretend as if I am opposing the celebrations. This means they are misrepresenting what you are saying. They are doing it deliberately. It is called an “ad hominem fallacy”: in simple words, shooting the messenger.

You have taken a strong stance on religion in our current times. Do you feel apprehensive?

If you take the specific example of [Pune-based rationalist] Narendra Dabholkar or even Galileo and Bruno, the cause for which they were fighting was expedited. Galileo and Bruno become martyrs for scientific temper.

And Dabholkar was fighting for an anti-superstition law to be passed for 18 years. But after his murder [in 2013], that law was passed immediately. The cause which he was fighting for got expedited. That’s why I am not fearful because I do not see the cause getting lost under any circumstances.

Here is a summary of last week’s top stories.

Costs for violating deportation rules. The Gauhati High Court directed the Assam government to pay Rs 2 lakh in compensation to the son of a Bengali-origin Muslim woman who was forced into Bangladesh. Jahanara Begum was declared a foreigner by a foreigners tribunal in 2019 and deported to Bangladesh in June.

The High Court passed a similar order in the case of Mumtaz Begum, who had also been forced out into Bangladesh, directing the state to pay her Rs 2 lakh in compensation.

These are the first instances in which the court has imposed costs on the state for forcing a person to Bangladesh in violation of deportation rules.

In a first, Gauhati HC asks Assam government to pay Rs 2 lakh to woman pushed into Bangladesh , reports Rokibuz Zaman.

Racism in the US. The United States’ Department of Homeland Security drew criticism for a social media post telling “Mr Singh” to “get off our roads” and accusing him of not knowing how to drive. Politicians and members of the Indian diaspora criticised the post as racist .

The artificial intelligence-generated image accompanying the post showed a brown-skinned man facing Transformers character Optimus Prime and carried the text: “Self-deport or find out.” Critics said that the post stereotyped people based on their surname and appearance.

The Hindu American Foundation and Coalition of Hindus of North America called for an investigation, while a Sikh-American politician in Michigan described it as “xenophobia dressed up as public policy”.

Concerns about AI. A researcher at artificial intelligence company Anthropic has quit, claiming that he is concerned the firm and the industry are racing to build AI systems that he believes they will not be able to control . In a series of social media posts on Wednesday, Jacob Coxon said that people should not underestimate the power of AI.

“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he said. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Anthropic has not yet commented on Coxon’s resignation, or on the concerns he raised.

Follow the Scroll channel on WhatsApp for a curated selection of the news that matters throughout the day, and a round-up of major developments in India and around the world every evening. What you won’t get: spam.

And, if you haven’t already, sign up for our Daily Brief newsletter.

editorials.title: ‘Under Water’: Tara Menon’s fragmented debut on grief and climate change never quite comes together
editorials.passage:
When the reader meets Marissa, the protagonist of Tara Menon’s Under Water , all that could happen to her has already happened. The banality of a new, if lax, life taxes her. A home awaits her – one she surely misses. She cannot fathom returning, though. It was in Thailand that a ravenous tsunami had gulped down Arielle, her once-infallible friend.

Six-year-old Arielle, upon meeting a freshly motherless Marissa, asserts that they can share hers. From then on, they share everything. They slice open a watermelon and eat it whole. Their teeth sink into fridge-cold mangoes. They bite into piping-hot pa thong ko slathered in condensed milk. They chug stolen bottles of Bacardi Breezers. For all their shared endeavours, what these two friends don’t seem to share is conversation; their banter is often laconic, even if the narration insists otherwise. No wonder, then, that Arielle, a literal apparition in half of the novel, is a literary apparition in the other. By the time she dies her inevitable death, I know her even less. To be a spirited, beautiful friend in Under Water is to be nothing more.

Such a truncated characterisation is perhaps par for the course for a novel that comes with a thesis: “So many people imagine that climate change, when it comes, will be spectacular,” Marissa preaches. “…But most of the time, devastation is quiet, subtle, humdrum.” In an interview, Menon parrots her character: “…climate change is imagined as something that will happen in the near or distant future, and when it does, it will be total and spectacular.” She writes Under Water as a “riposte” to the dominating assumption that has prevailed in her genre of choice. What Menon doesn’t defend as carefully is her style of choice.

The fragmentary novel, like the Impressionist painting, is composed of blotches that the seeing eye is obliged to bring together. For Menon, it seems that fragmentation is the appropriate treatment for a subject as misunderstood as grief. Indeed, she is right that it is not considered “acceptable to endlessly grieve” for a friend. In the face of her grief over Arielle, Marissa is often asked, “Were you in love with her?”, to which she bristles: “As if that could be the only explanation for this kind of grief.” For a book that wishes to remedy this misapprehension, Under Water is too distracted, burdening itself with marketable productivity, which, for a novel, is as good as death. (If you haven’t caught on, it is also about a “friendship [that] is already running out of time,” a friendship between women, at that. How the sales team must’ve rested easy.)

The structure of the novel, which flits between before Arielle’s death (Thailand) and after Arielle’s death (New York), is uniform in tone. That Menon wants the “…Thailand sections to feel light and beautiful, and the New York sections to feel dark and heavy” cannot be discerned. As with the Thailand sections, trivia, now chiefly on the Western canon, abounds, this time with the stated intent to demonstrate how Marissa’s loneliness shrinks her imagination to solely the literary: “…if she hadn’t lost Arielle, the years of college would have been extraordinarily social.”

Marissa, it is worth noting, is not of an entirely different temperament in the Thailand sections. There, too, her imagination is literary, if anything, pretentiously precocious. In the occasional paragraph in the Thailand sections where the reader forgets the looming ruination, the narration withholds, and its austerity gains the characteristic weight of its New York counterpart. That Marissa appears arrested in her teenage angst seems less the product of writerly control than mere happenstance.

Through its fragmentation, many of the novel’s sections reach for significance they never assume. Here is Marissa deliberately rubbing chilli-stained fingertips on her person. There are the gullible dodos that make for Dutch sailors’ meat. Look here, an etymological lesson on how pitcher plants acquired their scientific name. We detour so often, gathering reams of trivia, all of it narratively justified by interactions with the many researchers the girls meet at Marissa’s father’s research station.

Sometimes, Under Water reads as though an essayist stopped midway through a draft to write a novel instead. Its braided structure demands that at least some chapters abandon the reader with an abrupt image, and they do: a butterflied squirrel on a pavement, a hawk “ripping out flesh” as it feasts on a pigeon, a mother kite that “stands guard” to protect its young, a black-and-white warbler that “lies face up in the grass, dead.” What all of these vignettes motivate is unclear. In its insubordination to clarity, the novel, so intent on articulating grief, constipates it.

Of course, a novelist can, and sometimes should, grant narrative free rein to put the reader to task. It is clear that Menon considers ecological loss and personal loss to structurally rouse the same category of denial, the belief that the hurt will leave if you ignore it. Unfortunately, in Under Water, it is these losses that compete for the already spartan narrative room. There isn’t enough here to read that competition as the point. Authorial choices, however well thought out and theoretically airtight, are only half the labour of writing a novel. The rest you must actually write.

Under Water, Tara Menon, Simon and Schuster India.

editorials.title: A monk, a funeral and the ugly truth about Bangladesh
editorials.passage:
Some photographs tell a story far more poignantly than a whole book — or even a series of books — ever could.

Remember the photograph of the young Vietnamese girl running naked after a napalm attack on her village, 26 miles outside Saigon. That Pulitzer Prize-winning frame of a terrified child fleeing her village captured the horror of the Vietnam War in a single image. Or even the famous — or infamous — photograph of a starving child and a vulture, taken in March 1993 in what is today South Sudan by South African photojournalist Kevin Carter. The image of a severely malnourished child collapsed on the ground, with a vulture lurking behind, exposed the horrors of the devastating famine gripping the region. Many people thought there were two vultures — one behind the child and another behind the camera!

Last week, Bangladesh produced another photograph that should disturb us.

Chinmoy Krishna Das, the Bangladeshi Hindu monk who had been in jail for nearly two years, was granted five hours’ parole to attend his mother’s funeral. Das was inconsolable. He wept like a child. His 71-year-old mother had died with one wish unfulfilled: to see her imprisoned son one last time. Bangladeshi authorities did not allow that meeting. They let the son out only after his mother was dead.

That photograph — of a Hindu monk breaking down beside his mother’s mortal remains — is more than an image of private grief. It is, for me, a portrait of what it increasingly means to be a Hindu in Bangladesh: vulnerable, insecure and fraught with uncertainties.

That does not mean all was well before 2024. According to a human-rights report released during the good old Sheikh Hasina years, Bangladesh witnessed more than 3,600 attacks on Hindus between 2013 and 2021. Sheikh Hasina had been in power since 2009.

Even during those years, violence would periodically erupt on one pretext or another, with a particular community invariably bearing the brunt. One of the worst episodes came in 2021, after a copy of the Quran was found at a Durga Puja pandal. It later emerged that a Muslim man had placed it there, but by then the damage had been done. According to The Daily Star, “117 Hindu temples or puja pandals and 301 shops/homes were also damaged”.

The othering of Hindus was already a grim and increasingly normalised feature of Bangladeshi life. Anti-minority violence occurred repeatedly, even if the state generally managed to prevent it from spiralling completely out of control. For minorities, the cumulative effect resembled a slow attrition — and a slow death.

Over the past 50 years, while the total population of the country has more than doubled, the number of Hindus in Bangladesh has dropped by around 7.5 million. And if a recent research by Dhaka University professor Abul Barkat is to be believed, “Thirty years from now, no Hindus will be left in Bangladesh should the current rate of exodus continue.” Prof Barkat, who has been researching for over three decades on the socio-economic and political reasons behind the minorities leaving the country, backs his research by saying that the “rate of exodus over the past 49 years points in that direction”.

The pre-2024 phase was, in that sense, closer to the title of American author Richard L. Benkin’s book on Bangladesh — “A Quiet Case of Ethnic Cleansing”. The operative word was “quiet”. Murders took place in the past too; properties were vandalised at regular intervals; and minorities were quietly leaving the country for safer refuge. It was just that the violence against Hindus in Bangladesh was often in a controlled environment — a slow death.

Since August 2024, the Jamaat-led Islamist forces that Sheikh Hasina had sought to contain for 15 years — sometimes successfully, sometimes not — have acquired far greater visibility and political space. And with their rise, even the pretence that the lives and rights of Bangladesh's minorities will be adequately protected appears to have weakened.

This discrimination has both Islamist and anti-Awami League dimensions. Bangladesh's Hindus have long been perceived as an Awami League vote bank. In the post-Sheikh Hasina political order, that association has made an already vulnerable minority even more exposed.

Coming back to Chinmoy Krishna Das, his plight recalls, in a very different historical setting, two of Hinduism's greatest monks: Adi Shankaracharya and Swami Vivekananda. Like Das, both retained a profound attachment to their mothers even after embracing sannyasa.

Adi Shankara, according to tradition, defied the conventions of renunciation to care for his ailing mother before her death. This breaking of the rules of asceticism invited the hostility of his Namboodiri kinsmen, who reportedly boycotted the funeral rites and refused even to help prepare the pyre. Shankara had to perform his mother’s last rites himself.

Vivekananda, too, could never put his mother out of his mind, even after becoming a global religious figure following his celebrated Chicago address in 1893. He repeatedly sought financial assistance from friends and followers to alleviate his mother’s hardships. Vivekananda's concern for her at the height of his spiritual standing did more than humanise him; it offered a particular understanding of monkhood. Like Adi Shankara, he did not believe that renouncing worldly attachment required the extinction of filial duty.

Chinmoy Das’ love and longing for his mother displayed a similar attachment — an attachment that occupies a moral and emotional space transcending the rules of the monastic order. The Bangladesh administration’s decision to deny a son the chance to meet his mother for the last time is as much a personal tragedy as it is an epitome of being a Hindu in Bangladesh.

A photograph alone cannot explain a country. Nor can one man’s grief settle every argument about that country’s politics. But sometimes a photograph reveals something that official statements, diplomatic communiqués and political rhetoric don’t. The image of Chinmoy Das mourning his mother is one such moment. And it tells, in no uncertain terms, that Dhaka is well and truly in the grip of Islamists.

The time has come for New Delhi to formulate its policies accordingly. If Islamist forces continue to acquire greater influence over the Bangladeshi state, Bharat will have to discard any lingering illusions about the trajectory of normal and normalised bilateral relations.

India-Bangladesh relations are not merely passing through another diplomatic rough patch. They stand at a crossroads. And the photograph of a monk crying beside his dead mother has shown us why.

(Utpal Kumar is the author of ‘Bharat Rising: Dharma, Democracy, Diplomacy’ and ‘Eminent Distorians: Twists and Truths in Bharat’s History’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The Delhi Declaration: India’s Brics moment of strategic diplomacy
editorials.passage:
The adoption of the New Delhi Declaration at the 18th Brics Summit marks an important diplomatic achievement for India. It reflects New Delhi’s ability to manage an increasingly diverse grouping at a time of geopolitical fragmentation, competing national interests and weakening confidence in existing structures of global governance. India’s fourth Brics chairship has therefore been significant not simply because it hosted another major summit, but because it demonstrated that New Delhi can build consensus among countries that frequently disagree on major international questions.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi described Brics as having reached a moment of “coming of age”, emphasising that the grouping should advance “not by opposing anyone, but by taking everyone along”. This formulation captures the central geopolitical character of India’s chairship. New Delhi has sought to strengthen Brics without turning it into an anti-Western coalition, while simultaneously giving greater political weight to the concerns of the Global South.
India’s Diplomatic Test
India assumed the Brics chair at a particularly difficult moment. The grouping has expanded considerably and now brings together countries with divergent political systems, strategic partnerships, economic priorities and regional rivalries. Managing such a grouping requires more than producing a declaration; it requires creating sufficient political space for consensus.

India’s approach was therefore deliberately practical. Its chairship focused on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability, while linking these themes to food and energy security, supply chains, technology, development, financial cooperation and reform of global institutions. More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were held during the chairship, extending the Brics agenda beyond the annual leaders’ summit.

The New Delhi Declaration reflects this effort. It calls for a more representative, responsive and effective multilateral system, including comprehensive reform of the United Nations and greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making. Importantly for New Delhi, Russia and China reiterated their support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the United Nations, including the Security Council. This provides India with a significant diplomatic outcome at a time when reform of the international system has become central to its foreign policy.
The Pahalgam Reference: A Diplomatic Achievement
Perhaps the most politically consequential aspect of the Declaration for India is its explicit condemnation of the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, which killed 26 people. Brics leaders reaffirmed that terrorism is criminal and unjustifiable and called for zero tolerance, the rejection of double standards in countering terrorism, action against terrorist safe havens, the disruption of terrorist financing and accountability for those responsible.

The significance lies not merely in the wording but in the consensus behind it. India succeeded in placing terrorism firmly within the Brics security agenda without allowing the declaration to become a bilateral indictment of any particular country. This was diplomatically important given the grouping’s expanded membership and divergent strategic relationships.

For India, this represents an evolution of its long-standing effort to make the principle of “zero tolerance” towards terrorism a global norm rather than an India-specific demand. Modi had earlier argued that condemnation of terrorism must be a matter of principle and not convenience. The New Delhi Declaration gives that argument a wider multilateral platform.
The Geopolitics of What the Declaration Does Not Say
The geopolitical significance of the Declaration also lies in what it deliberately avoids. Ukraine and the Black Sea are not mentioned by name, despite their broader consequences for energy, food, shipping and global security. Rather than allowing one conflict to dominate the document, Brics adopted broader language on international tensions, conflict prevention, dialogue, diplomacy and peaceful resolution.

This is consistent with India’s broader diplomatic strategy. New Delhi has sought to preserve space for engagement with competing centres of power rather than align Brics with one geopolitical camp. The Declaration’s emphasis on multilateralism, sovereignty, peaceful resolution and reform therefore enables countries with sharply different positions to remain within a common framework.

The same balancing act is visible in the Declaration’s treatment of West Asia, where Brics called for maximum restraint and expressed concern over continuing escalation. In geopolitical terms, India succeeded in keeping the document focused on principles and collective interests rather than forcing members into rigid positions on every conflict.
From Global South Representation to Rule-Shaping
The deeper objective of India’s chairship has been to move the Global South from being primarily a recipient of global decisions to becoming a participant in shaping them. PM Modi’s formulation that the Global South is often in the “front row of global crises, but back row of decision-making” captures this concern.

The Declaration accordingly places considerable emphasis on reform of the UN, IMF, World Bank and WTO, while strengthening the role of developing and emerging economies. India has also sought to connect political reform with practical economic cooperation through digital public infrastructure, technology, innovation, supply-chain resilience, food and energy security and the New Development Bank.

This is where the Indian chairship has acquired geopolitical relevance. Brics is not being presented merely as an alternative institutional bloc, but as a platform through which emerging powers can seek greater agency within the existing international system.
India’s Brics Presidency: From Hosting to Delivering
India’s success should therefore not be measured simply by the adoption of a consensus declaration. Its greater achievement lies in demonstrating that it can manage geopolitical diversity without sacrificing strategic priorities. Securing consensus on Pahalgam, advancing India’s Security Council aspirations, retaining focus on Global South representation, and simultaneously avoiding an explicitly anti-Western posture required considerable diplomatic balancing.

The New Delhi Declaration thus strengthens India’s credibility as a bridge-builder and agenda-setter. It reinforces the proposition that strategic autonomy does not mean strategic ambiguity; rather, it means possessing sufficient diplomatic space to engage different powers while advancing clearly defined national and global interests.

India has emerged from its Brics presidency with an important lesson — its influence will increasingly depend not on choosing between competing geopolitical camps, but on its capacity to bring them into conversations where consensus remains difficult but necessary. The New Delhi Declaration is, in that sense, not merely a document of Brics consensus. It is a demonstration of India’s growing ability to shape the terms of that consensus.

(Dr. Indrani Talukdar is a Fellow at the Chintan Research Foundation, New Delhi. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The great oil pivot: India rewrites the global energy order
editorials.passage:
The global energy map has been redrawn, and the numbers tell the story. By mid-2026, India’s imports of Russian crude oil hit a record 2.8 million barrels per day (bpd), making up over half — 55.5 per cent — of the country's total crude intake. Next door, China pulled in another 2.4 million bpd.

Combined, this Asian energy axis is absorbing up to 85 per cent of Russia’s seaborne crude exports. What started as an opportunistic grab for discounted oil has morphed into a Russia-India-China (RIC) energy troika. This arrangement isn't just rerouting tankers across the Indian Ocean; it’s laying the physical groundwork for an expanded Brics+ and a parallel global economy.

When geopolitical lines showed fissures three years ago, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government responded with pragmatism. New Delhi’s refusal to cave in to Washington’s tariff threats wasn't an anti-Western rebellion. It was a straightforward calculation of national interest. By securing cheap oil for 1.4 billion citizens while simultaneously deepening defence ties with the US and Europe, India did more than protect its own economy. It inadvertently stabilised global energy markets and showed exactly where Western economic coercion hits a wall.
The Great Refining Irony
The speed of this shift is hard to overstate. Before the Ukraine war, Russia accounted for less than 100,000 bpd of Indian imports — a mere 2.5 per cent. Within two years, Russian Urals became the anchor of India's energy supply, with post-war spending on Russian crude topping $140 billion.

Then came the catch. Indian refiners processed this discounted crude into diesel and jet fuel, loaded it onto tankers, and shipped it straight to European and American ports. In doing so, India plugged the fuel deficits created by Western embargoes. Europe essentially paid a premium for Indian-refined fuel to keep the optics of its sanctions intact, allowing Indian refiners to post record margins while keeping Western petrol stations supplied.
Washington’s Quiet Consensus
You have to look past the political theatre in Washington to see how this really worked. Publicly, Capitol Hill was loud, issuing bipartisan threats of secondary tariffs of up to 500 per cent, alongside Donald Trump’s usual vows of steep duties.

Behind closed doors, however, Western technocrats knew the maths. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and other officials designed the G7 price cap specifically to keep Russian oil flowing. Taking 5 million barrels off the market overnight would have triggered a global supply shock. Former US Ambassador to India Eric Garcetti even admitted it publicly: "They bought Russian oil because we wanted somebody to buy Russian oil at a price cap... we didn't want the oil prices going up, and they fulfilled that."

India wasn't breaking the system; it was doing exactly what Western strategists needed it to do.
Calling Out the Double Standard
As political pressure mounted, New Delhi held its ground. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar famously dismissed the criticism by noting that Europe needed to outgrow the mindset that “its problems are the world’s problems, but the world’s problems are not Europe’s problems”.

Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri pointed out the obvious maths: if India had joined European buyers in competing for West Asian oil, global crude prices would have easily shot past $130 a barrel, risking severe global stagflation. The moral outrage also felt hypocritical to many in the Global South. The European Union was still conducting tens of billions of euros in trade with Moscow, and the US quietly kept buying Russian uranium, palladium and fertilisers.

This stance resonated across Eurasia. Russian President Vladimir Putin praised India’s independence, and Beijing — despite its ongoing border tensions with New Delhi — backed India's rejection of extraterritorial sanctions. Without ever signing a formal treaty, this informal RIC alignment absorbed enough trade to render unilateral Western sanctions largely ineffective.
The Brics Engine: Institutionalising the Pivot
The real legacy of this oil pivot goes far beyond shipping routes. It is actively rewiring the global economy.

This RIC energy axis gave Brics+ the momentum it needed to expand. By bringing major producers like the UAE and Iran into the fold, the expanded Brics bloc now controls about 43 per cent of global crude oil production and nearly half of the world's proven reserves.

This shift in oil control mirrors a broader economic shift. Brics+ now makes up more than 36 per cent of global GDP on a purchasing power parity basis, outpacing the G7’s 30 per cent share. With India and China expected to drive nearly 70 per cent of new global energy demand through 2040, energy pricing power is moving from the West to Eurasia.

Moving all this oil required new financial channels. To bypass Western banks and maritime insurance, these countries started trading outside the petrodollar. Today, more than 85 per cent of bilateral Eurasian energy trade is settled in UAE dirhams, Chinese yuan, Russian roubles and Indian rupees. What started as an emergency workaround has matured into a permanent, parallel financial system, complete with its own maritime underwriters and a shadow fleet immune to G7 rules.
The Blueprint for a Multipolar World
Perhaps the most striking part of PM Modi’s foreign policy is that India has managed to secure its energy needs without burning bridges with the West. Even as India helped anchor this new Eurasian energy bloc and gave Brics+ real economic teeth, New Delhi kept expanding its role in the Quad. It deepened defence manufacturing with US and European partners and locked in critical agreements on semiconductors and AI through the US-India Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET). And, yes, the bilateral trade deal, though much delayed, is actively in the works.

India proved that multi-alignment isn’t just about sitting on the fence. It’s about aggressively leveraging your position in a divided world. By anchoring the RIC energy troika, turning Brics+ into a real economic counterweight, and still holding on to its strategic partnerships with the West, India didn’t just survive a geopolitical crisis. It wrote the playbook for how to operate in a multipolar world.

(Rakesh Khar is a seasoned editor. He writes at the intersection of politics, business, technology and society. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: A Law in Search of a Problem: Why Goa Pulled Back on the Anti-Conversion Bill
editorials.passage: Senior advocate Cleofato Almeida Coutinho asked why Goa, a state with no cases of forced conversion, needed a strident anti-conversion law. He suggested that Goa needed an anti-superstition statute instead. Prabhakar Timble, educationist and former State Election Commissioner, warned that an anti-conversion law would create nurseries for self-appointed enforcers rather than solve any social problem, and Uday Bhembre, who has spent a lifetime participating in Goan public debate, pointed out to everyone that the Constitution already guarantees the right to change one’s religion.But it was not these sane and mature voices that made Chief Minister Pramod Sawant, who had chaired the 26 August Cabinet meeting which cleared the Goa Prohibition of Unlawful Conversion of Religion Bill, 2026, then five days later, minutes before the monsoon session of the Legislative Assembly opened, remove it from the Business List.Goa had come within hours of becoming the 14th state with an anti-conversion law on its statute book and possibly among the harshest in the country.This law is a key political objective of the party and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). The Narendra Modi government has encouraged every Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in the states to enact this law because it does not have the parliamentary strength to bring in a national legislation which would require a Constitutional amendment.Chhattisgarh's New Anti-Conversion Law Out-Hardlines BJP StandardsChief Minister Sawant blinked because key BJP leaders in the state had told him and the Prime Minister’s Office that the party would be badly hit in the coming elections, and the state exchequer would suffer irreparable injury if tourist-hungry Goa came to be known as intolerant and inhospitable to Christians.Hinduism is the majority religion of Goa at roughly 66 percent to 67 percent, Christians make up about 25 percent, while Muslims account for about 8 percent to 8.3 percent of the population. Christians are distributed unevenly across the state's two districts, with South Goa registering about 36 percent and North Goa about 16.4 percent.Goa is also perhaps the only state with a sizeable number of Christian MLAs on the government benches, and a very vocal civil society, and with between seven and 12 Catholic legislators supporting Sawant reportedly making their position clear before the session began, it was the arithmetic of a 40-member Assembly that made the Chief Minister, the state party president, and the national BJP leadership collectively retreat.Michael Lobo, who represents Calangute, said the Cabinet had acted in haste, the Bill required further study, everyone’s views needed to be considered, and matters were moving in the wrong direction. Delilah Lobo of Siolim confirmed that the government had agreed not to introduce it.Aleixo Reginaldo Lourenco, the Curtorim Independent who has sustained this government through some of its more difficult moments, made the sharpest point. The state’s own data, he said, showed no instances of forced conversion in Goa. He would, therefore, oppose the Bill on the floor unless it was first referred to a Select Committee. Antonio Vas of Cortalim had called for its outright withdrawal several days earlier.The Catholic Church and the Christian community reacted first with disbelief, and then with anger, with the Council for Social Justice and Peace and the Catholic Association of Goa, affiliated to the 107-year-old All India Catholic Union, issuing a joint statement on 27 August that the Bill risked replacing mutual trust with suspicion and social harmony with surveillance.Responding to questions from Yuri Alemao and, later, Carlos Ferreira, the Chief Minister told the Assembly that two conversion cases had been registered in 2022 and two more in 2023. That amounts to four cases in 14 years in a state of approximately 15.9 lakh people.The FIRs against Dominic D’Souza and Joan Mascarenhas were quashed by the Goa Bench of the Bombay High Court after Mapusa police filed a final summary conceding that, despite what the investigating officer described as considerable effort, no specific evidence had emerged against the accused. A third case was closed by the police themselves.This was the data on which the government intended to erect a statute providing, in some circumstances, for imprisonment extending to the end of a person’s life; a minimum fine of Rs 50,000; compensation of up to Rs 5 lakh; and imprisonment of between three and ten years for any priest, maulvi or “karmakandi” involved. The Bill also required 60 days’ notice to the authorities before a conversion, during which relatives and third parties could file objections. The provision of making marriages void where a court concluded that conversion had been their purpose is very popular with BJP governments, each of which has introduced it in existing or new laws, specifically directed against the tiny Muslim population, and visitors.Writing in the Sangh’s own weekly two days before the withdrawal, an advocate of the Bill relied not on conversion cases in Goa but on the increase in the Muslim share of the population, from 1.95 percent in 1960 to 8.33 percent in 2011, and on disputes in Kerala concerning Waqf land and interfaith marriage.This was a shameful admission that the government, with all the BJP and RSS cadres at its command, apart from the intelligence network of the police with a tiny population to watch could not find a Goan Christian to accuse and instead had to evoke the Sangh’s demographic anxiety to justify its actions.The Christian share of Goa’s population fell from 38.07 percent at the last Portuguese census to 25.10 percent in 2011. The absolute number of Christians barely changed in the decade to 2011, rising from 359,568 to 366,130, while the state’s total population continued to grow.In Salcete, the Christian heartland, Christians constituted three-quarters of the taluka’s population in 1961. Their proportion has since steadily declined because of in-migration and departure. In Mormugao, the Christian share collapsed from 54 percent to 22 percent. Whatever is reshaping Goa’s religious composition, it is not conversion to Christianity. Maharashtra’s New Conversion Law Doesn’t Regulate Faith. It Empowers the MobWhile the government prepared to require 60 days’ notice from a Goan wishing to change faith, Goans have been changing their nationality in tens of thousands, without ceremony. Sawant told the Assembly that 25,939 people had surrendered Indian passports in Goa during the decade ending in March 2024. Official estimates place the figure at 26,612 between 2015 and 2025, following 11,500 during the five years ending in 2013.The Portuguese consulate in Panaji has 15,655 registered electors, compared with 349 at the embassy in Delhi, and an estimated 8,000 Goans live in the Wiltshire city of Swindon alone. The state’s demographic crisis is one of emigration and dispossession, of land conversions under Section 39-A, and of an economy that offers educated young people little they want. The electoral map explains the real issue with clarity—24 of Goa’s 40 Assembly constituencies lie within the four Old Conquest talukas of Salcete, Bardez, Tiswadi, and Mormugao. Excluding the four urban seats of Margao, Mormugao, Panaji, and Mapusa, the remaining 20 have Christian populations ranging from 40 to 90 percent.According to estimates by the BJP’s own organisers, Salcete’s eight constituencies are approximately 85 percent Catholic and have never, in three decades, been friendly territory for the party. In 2024, the Congress won South Goa by 61,000 votes against a candidate as well-resourced as Pallavi Dempo. Calangute and Siolim belong to the Lobos, Santa Cruz to Rodolfo Fernandes, Aldona to Carlos Ferreira, and Panaji and Taleigao to the Monserrate family.The template of these anti-conversion laws, though loosely based on the first one enacted in Orissa in 1967, appears to have been worked out as far back as 2014 in the RSS headquarters in Nagpur or New Delhi, with each draft fine-tuned for the circumstances of the state where it was meant to apply, and then enacted. By now, the tally is 13, with as many as eight states enacting the legislation after 2014, including Uttar Pradesh.The doctrinal position remains where the Supreme Court left it in 1977 in Rev Stainislaus: the right to propagate religion under Article 25 does not include the right to convert another person, but the newer statutes go far beyond that holding, requiring prior notice to a district magistrate, burden of proof onto the convert, and criminalising the pastor or alluvia.Petitions challenging these laws have been pending since 2020, led by Citizens for Justice and Peace and joined by the National Council of Churches in India and the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India. The Court issued notice to the Union and to 12 states in February this year.The asymmetry at the centre of these statutes remains both unaddressed and unembarrassed. No government of this party, at the Centre or in any state, has criminalised reconversion to Hinduism, although “Ghar Wapsi” deploys precisely the promises of caste status, reservation and employment that the statutes define as "allurement."It is clear, as civil society often says, that these laws do not prohibit conversion; they prohibit one direction of religious travel.Goa’s place in this story contains a further irony, as its Portuguese-era Civil Code of 1867 is repeatedly cited from national platforms as evidence that a uniform civil code is workable in India. Uttarakhand, Gujarat and Assam have legislated their own versions on that argument. Christian churches believe the Bill has been parked, not scrapped, as nothing in the Chief Minister’s conduct suggests that he has abandoned it. Moreover, the assurance given on 31 August extended only to a three-day session.The Bill will probably return after 2027, when the electoral arithmetic may no longer require the support of seven Catholic legislators. A Bill withdrawn for want of votes is not a Bill defeated, and the next Assembly may supply what this one would not.(The author is a writer and activist. He is the former President of the 102-year-old All India Catholic Union. This is an opinion piece. The views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for them.)

editorials.title: Sweden Votes, Why India Should Pay Attention
editorials.passage: For most Indian readers, Sweden appears only intermittently in public debates – as the land of welfare, gender equality, clean cities, IKEA, Volvo, Spotify, Nobel prizes, Greta Thunberg, and occasionally Bofors. Scandinavian politics rarely enters India’s everyday geopolitical imagination. Compared to the United States, Britain, Russia, China, West Asia and increasingly Japan or Australia, the Nordic countries are usually treated as politically stable and strategically distant. Sweden’s 2026 election should unsettle that assumption. On 13 September 2026, Sweden will elect its national parliament, the Riksdag, along with municipal and regional councils. The Riksdag (Parliament) has 349 seats, elected through a proportional system in which parties generally need at least 4 per cent of the national vote to enter parliament. The election will be the first since Sweden joined NATO in March 2024, ending its long attachment to military non-alignment. It also comes only months after Narendra Modi’s visit to Gothenburg in May, when India and Sweden elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership. The two governments have set an objective of doubling bilateral trade and investment within five years, against the wider backdrop of the recently concluded India–EU Free Trade Agreement. Sweden’s domestic political choices therefore intersect more directly with Indian interests than the geographical distance might suggest. What does Sweden’s election reveal about the changing political grammar of the democratic West, and why should India and South Asia care? The first reason is the future of the Nordic welfare state under right-populist pressure. Sweden has long been central to the idea of the “social democratic welfare regime”, where universal social rights, high taxation, labour organisation and state capacity produced a distinctive social compact (Esping-Andersen, 1990; Hilson, 2008). The model was never as homogeneous as its admirers imagined. Yet it still embodied a political imagination in which welfare was not charity but based on citizenship. That imagination is now under strain. Since 2022, Sweden has been governed by a centre-right minority government led by Ulf Kristersson’s Moderates, with the Christian Democrats and Liberals, and dependent on the Sweden Democrats through the Tidö Agreement. It is important to note here that the Sweden Democrats is a party usually classified in comparative politics as part of the European radical right. Mainstream Swedish parties historically maintained a strict cordon sanitaire around the Sweden Democrats. The party was founded in 1988 by Nazi sympathizers and figures from the far-right skinhead movement. But in 2026 the institutional horizon of the Tidö agreement has been changed. Kristersson has opened the door to a four-party government that would include the Sweden Democrats if the right retains power, while Jimmie Åkesson, the leader of Sweden Democrats, has said his party expects substantial ministerial influence. The election is therefore also about whether a radical-right party that has shaped policy from outside government crosses the final threshold into cabinet. Beyond Presser Row, Modi's Scandinavia Visit Brought Focus on Democratic DeclineThe Sweden Democrats have already helped move Swedish politics from welfare universalism towards welfare conditionality, migration restriction and cultural belonging. The pattern has recognisable South Asian resonances. Across democracies, welfare and majoritarian politics increasingly travel together. Welfare is not necessarily abolished. It is moralised. The question becomes not simply who is vulnerable, but who is deserving, assimilable, nationally loyal and administratively legible. In Sweden, this logic has become increasingly concrete. Since June, the general residence requirement for citizenship has risen from five to eight years, alongside new self-sufficiency and knowledge requirements. The country held its first citizenship test on Swedish society in August. Since July, stricter rules on vandel, or good conduct, have also allowed immigration authorities to consider whether residence-permit applicants are law-abiding, support themselves honestly and do not threaten public order. The contexts differ sharply from India, but the political move is very much comparable. Welfare, citizenship and belonging increasingly sit on the same continuum. The same impulse is visible in Sweden’s cultural canon. In September 2025, a government-appointed committee proposed 100 works, objects, ideas and social practices deemed central to Swedish cultural heritage. The government presented the canon as a common cultural reference for new and established citizens. Critics saw a more exclusionary question underneath it: what counts as Swedish, whose history enters the national story, and whose remains peripheral. In 2026, the canon moved beyond debate and was implemented. The government instructed the National Agency for Education to examine how it could be incorporated into school steering documents, while the National Heritage Board was tasked with developing a digital platform for its dissemination. From the South Asian perspective, the resonance is difficult to miss. Debates over textbooks, heritage, civilisational identity and minority belonging have become central to Indian politics. Sweden’s canon is not an Indian analogue, but it demonstrates how culture can become a political technology of belonging. Once the nation formally defines the cultural knowledge through which membership is imagined, migration ceases to be only about visas and borders. It becomes a question of who can enter the nation’s moral community. This has immediate consequences for South Asia. Sweden is a destination for students, IT professionals, researchers, engineers and families. Indian government data counted about 91,600 overseas Indians in Sweden in early 2026. Since 1 June, Sweden has also tightened its work-permit regime. The general salary threshold is now 90 per cent of the national median salary, currently SEK 34,470 per month, although exemptions apply to specified groups and occupations. An election in Sweden can therefore affect Indian mobility not only through visas, but through the political definition of the “valuable” migrant. Swedish politics also has wider implications across South Asia. In June, Stockholm adopted a new development-cooperation strategy for Bangladesh for 2026–31, allowing Sida to spend approximately SEK 200 million annually on democratic development, rights, women’s empowerment, green transition and climate resilience. The strategy also explicitly describes development cooperation as an instrument of foreign policy that can advance Swedish interests and priorities. Sweden has not abandoned internationalism, but its older humanitarian self-image is increasingly being reorganised through security, trade, migration management and national interest. Security is the third reason to watch the election. NATO membership transformed Sweden from a militarily non-aligned Nordic state into a formal part of the Euro-Atlantic security architecture. For India, which balances relations with Russia, the United States and Europe while invoking strategic autonomy, the change matters. The new India–Sweden partnership includes defence dialogue, cyber policy, counterterrorism cooperation and defence innovation. The election will not reverse NATO membership. Sweden’s rearmament now rests on unusually broad parliamentary agreement, with all Riksdag parties backing the expansion of defence. Elections will shape priorities and trade-offs, but not the fundamental strategic turn. For India, Sweden is useful precisely because it shows how medium powers are adapting to a harsher geopolitical order. The fourth reason is climate and industrial transition. The India–Sweden partnership identifies cooperation in green steel, cement, transport, energy storage, smart grids and sustainable mining. India’s industrial future will increasingly be shaped by decarbonisation pressures, EU carbon regulation, green supply chains and technological standards. After another summer of extreme heat in Europe, climate has also returned more visibly to Sweden’s electoral debate. The question for India is not whether Sweden can “teach” India sustainability, but whether Swedish technology and capital can interact with Indian scale, manufacturing capacity and developmental needs on genuinely reciprocal terms. Finally, the election is about democracy itself. Sweden remains institutionally strong, but it is entering the final weeks of the election campaign shaped by debates on welfare, crime, migration, security and belonging. An August SVT/Verian poll placed the four opposition parties at 53.9 per cent against 43.9 per cent for the Tidö parties. The Liberals polled at 1.9 per cent, well below the 4 per cent parliamentary threshold. Polls are not predictions. But the possibility of a change of government is real, while the fate of a small party could decisively reshape coalition arithmetic. Sweden’s election is therefore not a morality play between enlightened Scandinavia and an illiberal elsewhere. It is a window into how liberal democracies are being remade from within by welfare nationalism, cultural bordering, migration control, security politics and geopolitical uncertainty. These forces are not alien to India. They travel through different histories and institutions, but pose comparable questions: who belongs, who is protected, who may move, what citizens must know, and who gets to define the nation. India should follow the upcoming Swedish election not because Stockholm sits at the centre of global geopolitics, but because Sweden is diagnostic. The distance between Stockholm and New Delhi now runs through migration offices, defence partnerships, technology corridors, green industry, universities, aid budgets and competing ideas of democratic belonging. Sweden’s 2026 election provides a different perspective on the political forces already shaping South Asia. It is to see, from another angle, a political world in which South Asia is already deeply entangled. (Niladri Chatterjee is a senior lecturer and researcher at Department of Cultural Sciences, Linnaeus University, Sweden and an affiliated researcher with University of Oslo, Norway.This is an opinion piece and the views expressed are the author’s own.
